records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 13 March 2026 Weekly view When in doubt, don’t In the middle of extreme uncertainty, four central banks in Europe (and a few more in the developed market world outside of Europe, including the Fed) will take decisions next week. Or rather, they won’t – with this level of uncertainty on the size and persistence of the energy price shock, we expect all of them to stay on hold. As we argued last week, there is option value in waiting. That means inaction next week, but communication will be watched closely for any hints about the future. We doubt we will get much guidance, but with markets in a hawkish mood, lack of guidance can easily be taken as hawkish. For now, in Europe, under a relatively quick resolution scenario, growth effects should be largely contained and our current calls for central banks would still hold. A persistent shock can have strong growth and inflation implications, as we discussed at length last week. It can delay cuts from both the BoE and the ECB, and even lead to hikes if the shock is large and/or persistent enough. The bar for ECB hikes, although quite high, is likely lower than for the BoE. ECB preview: risk of hawkish no communication The ECB is likely to hold rates next week, but the key focus will be its communication, which should stress rising inflation risks, weakening growth, and unusually high uncertainty – effectively a hawkish tilt despite offering no forward guidance. The disruption shows no signs of stabilizing even after our initial assumption of a 10-day duration has passed. Our commodities team now expects the disruption to last for longer. Its new baseline scenario assumes that SoH oil flows will remain at 10% of normal levels for 21 days until March 20, revising our oil price forecast accordingly. The team now expects the Brent oil price to initially rise to $110/bbl during the ongoing disruptions in March. It then looks for a decline to the $80-$85 range in April-May, but estimates the average Brent price for the March-May period will be at least 30% higher than the 2025 average ($68). Subsequently, we expect the price to stabilize at $71 in Q4 2026, but remain slightly above the 2025 average. We also expect attempts to be made to ease supply constraints, including the release of strategic petroleum reserves by IEA members. Energy Upside Tilts Yield Risks to the Downside The energy price spike resulting from the strikes on Iran have shaken rates markets out of the prevailing low vol regime, with renewed focus on the potential for negative supply shocks to result in a combination of higher inflation and lower growth. Our economists’ forecast revisions point in this direction, with central banks previously close to cutting likely to delay cuts, those previously firmly on hold likely to see the pricing of hike risk, and those hiking—especially the RBA—potentially even accelerating hikes. However, despite this upward shift in the distribution for very front-end rates, we think that the downward revisions to growth—especially in markets with softer labor markets—point to lower yields eventually, with the outlook for 10y yields now more asymmetric to the downside. However, he could have more influence in maintaining a status quo policy, e.g., by keeping policy on hold rather than raising rates in borderline cases. At the margin, we therefore view changes in Fed composition as further leaning against rate hikes this year. KBRA's rating for the EU reflects the creditworthiness of the EU’s key MS and their commitment to ensuring the continued soundness of the EU’s finances, based on the balanced budget principle and a legally enshrined debt service priority. These factors, combined with significant budgetary flexibility - including recourse to additional timely member support if and when needed, which functions like a joint and several guarantee - are key to the EU’s credit profile. We highlight that EU bonds do not benefit from an explicit “joint and several guarantee" by EU MS, i.e. investors do not have a direct legal claim against MS they can use in court in case EU bonds are not paid in full and in time. However, as suggested by KBRA, the EU indeed benefits from “joint and several support”, i.e. MS must provide further support to the EU budget if necessary. This will also support bondholders, of course. According to KBRA, the EU has a proven track record of excellent governance and an irreplaceable mandate for its member states, which has been reinforced by the bloc’s response to the pandemic and to the Russia-Ukraine war. The following day, his remarks that the end of the war was near led to a reversal into twist-flattening, after which yields continued to swing on Middle East headlines. In particular, the labor market likely needs to re-tighten – e.g., with the unemployment rate falling back towards 4%, quits rising, and wages accelerating, among other conditions – and, therefore, return as a source of inflationary pressures. Second, core PCE likely needs to show evidence of accelerating noticeably above 3%. Furthermore, the source of the rise cannot be readily identifiable as a shock that is likely to prove transitory even in the absence of tighter monetary policy (e.g., tariffs or oil). Of course, there may be thresholds for core inflation where the source of the rise is down-weighted. Nonetheless, to get to hikes the Fed would have to discard a strongly held narrative that a disinflationary trend is in place and that once one-off shocks dissipate inflation will be close to 2%. This would take a compelling story. Clearly, realization of the first point (a re-tightening labor market) would be one reason to reconsider fundamental assumptions about the disinflation trend. As always, inflation expectations feature as a wildcard in this assessment. If measures of long-run inflation expectations began to rise noticeably, it would lower the thresholds on the labor market and spot inflation required for the Fed to consider a hike. Reference Month Selection Selecting an appropriate reference month is essential to balancing timeliness with data completeness. Fund disclosure is inherently staggered: portfolio snapshots are released with a lag, and reporting frequencies vary; some funds report monthly, others quarterly or less frequently. As a result, the breadth of available data fluctuates from month to month. In practice, we designate a reference month that is typically the end of the previous- previous month relative to the publication date. This convention reflects a pragmatic compromise: the most recent month-end is generally too sparsely covered to support robust analysis, while the second-most recent month offers sufficient breadth to be representative of institutional positioning, without being so dated that insights lose relevance. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy A crude awakening With oil prices scaling the $100/bbl level, Euribors failed to catch a break this week again. ECB speakers called for vigilance given upside risks to inflation. The set-up for next week's policy meeting(s) is hawkish but hike premium can build further. We recommend going long belly of EUR2s5s10s fly Curve ball from the Strait. For anyone expecting a quick de-escalation to the Iran conflict, this week proved to be another disappointment. If last week Euribors were roiled by the surge in gas prices, this week it was their turn to slip and slide on oil. After the wild ride in crude prices on Monday, which saw a peak of $120/bbl before retracing, oil prices have repeatedly tried to scale that $100/bbl level. Naturally, these price developments again weighed on the STIR complex with SOFRs, ERs and SFIs all being hit, although the scale of the increase was less than the previous week. Our economics teams have explored what $100/bbl oil could imply for Europe and other key economies (see Assessing the Middle East fallout). If the conflict persists for several more weeks, they expect real GDP growth to fall and inflation to rise, with the magnitude of revisions conditional on the peak and persistence in energy prices. They expect fiscal authorities to implement measures to cushion households and firms from the energy shock and for the ECB and BoE to react quicker than they did after the Russia-Ukraine conflict began, albeit more gradually.

records.text: For the S&P 500, the earnings headwind from softer GDP growth in our baseline outlook will be offset by a tailwind from AI investment spending. The net effect of higher oil prices on S&P 500 EPS is roughly neutral, but our economists’ reduced GDP growth forecasts shaves roughly 1 pp off of our previous 2026 EPS growth forecast. However, the outlook for 2026 AI investment spending has continued to surprise to the upside and is on track to contribute over 1/3 of S&P 500 EPS growth this year. In addition, with 4Q 2025 earnings fully reported, 2025 EPS came in slightly above our estimates. As a result, we maintain our base case forecast for 12% EPS growth in 2026 (to $309) and 10% growth in 2027 ($342), but those growth rates now indicate slightly higher levels of EPS than our previous estimates. Our revised 2026 forecast is similar to the median top-down strategist but below the bottom-up consensus. Our 2027 EPS estimate is also below the bottom-up consensus, as we believe analyst forecasts for broad-based margin expansion and EPS acceleration next year are unrealistic. By the end of 2026, there should be greater clarity regarding the war with Iran and the trajectory of the Fed, but uncertainty surrounding the impact of AI will likely remain, maintaining pressure on valuation multiples. That seems a very narrow landing strip to us. That required combination may prove wishful thinking if Hormuz disruption is prolonged, because the macro tail is exactly the “non-linear” one where the growth shock dominates. Time to wrap up. Yes, inflation will rise. Whether this will translate into ECB hikes will depend on two factors: how persistent the inflation spike can be expected to be, and whether a meaningful slowdown in global growth is likely. We think that, compared to just one week ago, risks to the growth outlook have significantly increased. The share of global oil supply at stake is ten times larger than the initial “2% of world supply” scale often discussed in 2022. The Strait is a critical global shipping lane: flows through Hormuz account for about one-fifth of global oil and petroleum product consumption and more than one-quarter of seaborne oil trade (see here). In early 2022, by contrast, the “effective removal” of oil supply was initially discussed to be in the order of ~2mb/d, roughly ~2% of global production (here). While the comparison is not perfect, it points to important differences in magnitude. The potential disruption to the world energy system is much bigger this time around than in 2022. A recession is likely if the Hormuz disruption becomes prolonged (see here). Despite the greater potential downside than in 2022, fiscal policy is less likely to repeat the 2022/23 playbook (see here). Under the baseline of a short-lived shock, there is little room for a fiscal expansion. Outside of a recession, any response would likely remain modest and targeted (<0.3pp of GDP). And while Europe did mobilise large energy-related support in 2022 (the euro area total is shown at ~1.8% of GDP in that year), the combination of higher financing costs and tighter fiscal constraints makes a repeat at that scale less likely. The ECB is, in principle, well equipped for this constellation of events. And the starting point matters. This would be broadly in line with/marginally above Bloomberg consensus estimates/market pricing. We see core CPI at 24bp month-on-month in seasonally-adjusted terms, which would be at a similar level as the average monthly inflation rate in the first nine months of last year (i.e. before the government shutdown related noise), though below the 30bp recorded in January. Core goods inflation is expected to have accelerated. Used cars CPI had surprised to the downside in January, and wholesale prices point to some recovery in February and further strength in March (Figure 8). Outside of cars, business surveys and PPIs suggest that indirect effects from higher tariff costs continue to put upward pressure on consumer prices. This is particularly true for clothing items; while import prices have recently eased again, producer prices for apparel products have risen strongly (Figure 9). Drug prices, finally, remain a downside risk. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley MUFG 15 Methodology Our analysis tracks positioning of actively managed mutual funds investing in Japan equities. Holdings data are taken from FactSet, aggregated into two cohorts (Japan Equity & Global Equity funds) and benchmarked vs. TOPIX 500 & MSCI Japan, respectively. Active Weight Calculation The key measure of fund positioning is active weight, which captures how an actively managed portfolio departs from its reference index. To calculate it, we construct an asset- weighted composite portfolio for each cohort at the end of every reporting month. Within each cohort, the market value of every parent-equity position is aggregated across all constituent funds, and expressed as a share of that cohort’s combined Japanese-equity assets under management. We then pair these fund weights with corresponding normalized weights of the relevant benchmark. Active weight is defined as the difference between the fund weight and the benchmark weight, measured in percentage points. A positive figure signals an overweight, and a negative figure an underweight. Repeating this calculation for consecutive disclosure periods allows us to capture month-on-month changes in conviction. Between official disclosure dates, each fund’s most recently reported holdings are projected forward and adjusted for asset price changes to approximate end-month positions. records.text: 3. Energy subsidy regimes. In most regional economies, governments have developed policies to shield consumers from the worst effects of energy price shocks. These can take a variety of forms, including fixed subsidy amounts, price stabilization/gradual adjustment, price caps, or simply long-term fixed prices. They can be funded on the regular fiscal budget or through mechanisms such as lower margins by SOEs operating in the energy sector. To illustrate the energy subsidy impact and the extreme degree of variation in pass-through, we present charts of electricity and motor fuel CPI data across EM Asian economies in the years surrounding the Covid pandemic and Ukraine invasion. Electricity prices range from nearly fixed in China, to large double-digit percentage fluctuations in Thailand and Malaysia, for example (Exhibit 4). Motor fuel prices are more correlated but even here there is significant variation (Exhibit 5). records.text: 2 Asia Economic Weekly | 13 March 2026 This Week in Focus Geopolitical risks remain the key focus in the region. In addition to the oil shock, Asia is exposed to heightened LNG shortage risks due to its heavy reliance on LNG imports, thin inventories, and vulnerability to supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. On the data front, China’s CPI inflation rose to a three year high, while Jan–Feb trade flows surged above expectations. In India, takeaways from recent macro tours suggest that the policy response is likely to be back loaded, with near term efforts focused on supply augmentation—particularly for LNG and LPG. In Japan, rising oil prices threaten the outlook for positive real wage growth, potentially weighing on household consumption. In Indonesia, the fiscal deficit widened in Feb, with pressures building amid higher oil prices. China: CPI inflation picked up to 3-year high; Jan-Feb trade soared CPI inflation rebounded notably to 1.3% yoy in Feb (up from 0.2% in Jan), reflecting LNY calendar shifts and the improvement in services prices. PPI deflation narrowed to -0.9% yoy (from -1.4% in Jan), mainly driven by firmer producer goods prices. Uncertainty around the inflation outlook has risen amid tensions involving Iran, given that over one third of China’s oil imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Over those 6 weeks, JULI spreads widened by 36bp to 168bp. The move wider was (somewhat paradoxically) led by Energy, which notably underperformed (+52bp over 6 weeks) despite higher oil prices, perhaps reflecting concerns that higher oil prices would lead to demand destruction and/or a recession. Exhibit 15: Correlations shift as the oil futures curve becomes downward sloping Source: Bloomberg, Morgan Stanley Research Therefore a further rise in short-term oil prices which drives the futures curve into deeper backwardation would likely weigh on EUR, particularly versus CHF. Conversely, a longer- term oil market disruption that sends futures prices higher along the curve would likely weigh on the EUR particularly versus NOK as changes in Europe and Norway's terms of trade affect medium-term growth expectations. Both of these scenarios are EUR-negative; our economists see lower GDP relative to their baseline in all three scenarios they consider here. They note that the negative impact on European GDP in the long-term disruption scenario may be particularly substantial - up to 2 percentage points. We would expect EUR to rise versus the USD in a de-escalation scenario in which oil prices decline, given EUR/USD's negative correlation to oil prices in conditions of deep backwardation. records.text: arch analyst account. Key Takeaways As geopolitical tension in the Middle East escalated, the JGB curve initially bear- steepened as popular flattener trades were unwound. Markets believe prolonged geopolitical escalation would make it difficult for the BoJ to hike in the very near term, while pricing higher term premium on the longer end given the risk of the BoJ falling behind the curve. That said, if tensions last longer than markets anticipate, we see a risk that growth concerns > inflation concerns at some point. In that event, we would see the JGB curve shifting from bear-steepening to twist- steepening, with long-end JGBs likely facing selling pressure from pension funds’ rebalancing. As such, we maintain the JGB 5s30s steepener. We also maintain receive April MPM OIS, as the BoJ would likely take time to assess the impact of higher energy prices on underlying inflation. From the base case of last week’s Inflation Watch, current market pricing of oil and gas would move our forecast up, and we would expect euro area HICP inflation to come in above 2.5%Y in 2026. Yet, if prices go down in line with current futures, it would again be below 2% in 2027. The main propagation channel is oil (our rule of thumb: a sustained $10/bbl increase in Brent lifts euro area HICP by ~40bp), and the quick pass-through of a large part of the shock is already in the news all over Europe: pump prices have increased significantly: +15% for diesel this week and 7% for euro super95. Growth will be hit too: the same sustained $10/bbl move shaves around 15bp off EA GDP. The channel here is mainly private consumption. Effects are spread over 2026– 27 (see here). In all this, the persistence of higher inflation remains the key unknown. Our inflation scenarios make that point clear: even under a “smoothed” baseline that assumes prices normalise in coming weeks, 2026 headline inflation rises slightly above the ECB’s target. More adverse energy paths take headline above 3%Y in 2026, with very different implications for 2027 depending on whether energy prices decline or remain high. records.text: 13 March 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week ahead ECB policy meeting (Thu) The upcoming ECB meeting on Thursday will be dominated by the recent surge in energy prices and the conflict in the Middle East. We think it is highly unlikely the ECB will change policy at this meeting. Instead, the focus will be on the messaging. We expect the Governing Council to acknowledge the increased uncertainty and the upside risks to near-term inflation, reiterate the flexibility of its current policy stance, and, most importantly, deliver a strong, resolute commitment to maintaining price stability. The key market signal will be the strength of the language used to underline this commitment, which could range from standard phrases to more hawkish "vigilance" rhetoric reminiscent of the Trichet era. Looking ahead, the path of monetary policy is contingent on the evolution of energy prices and the risk of persistent inflation. Our baseline scenario, which holds for now, is for the ECB to keep rates at 2% through 2026 before hiking in mid-2027 as domestic tailwinds begin to dominate. However, the risks are significant. The report outlines two key scenarios: a moderate, transitory energy shock ($80/bbl and gas at EUR50/MWh) that the ECB could 'look through', and a more adverse scenario with a 50% rise in energy costs ($120/bbl and gas at EUR75/MWh) that would likely trigger a recession and a persistent inflation overshoot, forcing a policy response. records.text: Our analysis suggests that we are unlikely to see material second-round effects in core inflation if energy prices normalise in coming weeks, as the increase in commodity prices (so far) is materially smaller than in 2022 (Exhibit 6). But the pass-through could increase materially if the energy shock continues to build. We therefore set out stylised scenarios for how energy prices, the economy and ECB policy might evolve from here (Exhibit 7). In our baseline forecast—where the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz ends after 21 days and energy prices subsequently normalise—we expect 1% Q4/Q4 growth this year (down from 1.4% before the conflict), headline inflation at 2.7% by 2026Q3 (vs 2.2%) and only slightly higher core inflation (up 0.2pp to 2.4% in 2026Q3). records.text: changed our BoE call and we no longer expect the Bank to cut Bank Rate at the next meeting on 19 March, instead delaying the decision to April, when the Bank will present updated macro projections. We also flagged a significant risk of further delays to our expectations of two cuts in April and July (to 3.25%). However, following a 0.4pp upward revision to our 2026 inflation forecast (to 2.4%) earlier this week, foreseeing above target inflation until August 2027, we have flagged a major risk of a delay in rate cuts, currently pencilled in for April and July, to H2 2026 or even early 2027. In this context, we also no longer expect any MPC members to vote for a cut at at the meeting next week. We see two factors that could bring interest rate cuts forward. First, a quick resolution of the conflict and a faster and larger than expected drop in energy prices than we currently assume. Second, a "light touch" fiscal response, e.g. a delay in the fuel duty hike (currently scheduled to take place in Sep-26 and Jan-27), limiting the increase in fuel prices and/or household energy bills. We see the bar for BoE hikes as relatively high. With Bank Rate at 3.75%, we think the majority of the MPC would still view this level as restrictive. Hence, we think that the MPC could limit the risk of second-round effects without necessarily hiking rates. This report has been prepared by UBS AG London Branch. records.text: M Idea 2 Core PCE inflation came in strong in 1Q, but deceleration is coming Our view that core PCE inflation would accelerate in 1Q26 was confirmed this week following February’s CPI print on Wednesday and today’s release of January PCE prices. January core PCE came in below expectations but still firm at 0.36% m/m (vs. 0.50% MS and 0.4% consensus), with strength across both services and goods. The downside surprise appears largely methodological: The key driver was legal services in PCE. Instead of the usual approach of inferring legal services from CPI (which would have implied roughly ~11% m/m in that category), the BEA appears to have leaned on PPI legal services instead (1.8% m/m). That choice likely shaved close to 10bp off core PCE. The main uncertainty is whether this methodological change persists in coming months. Following the CPI print, we are now tracking February core PCE at 0.42%, pointing to another firm reading. If our forecasts are correct, these two prints would push the 3 month and 6 month annualized pace of core PCE to 4.67% and 3.54% in February, respectively—elevated sequential inflation rates. More specifically, within the services sector wholesale and retail trade (+1% m/m) was the largest positive contributor, while administrative and support services (-2.3% m/m), particularly employment activities, were the main drag. Industrial output contracted 0.1% m/m in January (after -0.9% m/ m in December) driven by declines in mining (-3.2% m/m) and energy (-0.4% m/m), while manufacturing output was slightly up (+0.1% m/m) and water supply jumped 1.9% m/m. Within the manufacturing sector, 5 out of 13 sub-sectors expanded in January, with the largest positive contribution coming from transport equipment (+4% m/m), while machinery and equipment (-7.7% m/m), electrical equipment (- 9% m/m) and computer and electronics (-2.8% m/m) were the main drags. In contrast, construction output was up 0.2% m/m (after -0.5% m/m in December), with the increase solely driven by an increase in repair and maintenance, while new works was down. Moreover, even if the tension in the Middle East eases and oil prices peak relatively quickly, it will remain necessary to keep a close eye on the price/economic impacts for a while. Accordingly, we think the possibility of an April rate hike is also diminishing. For the time being we think BoJ monetary policy will be a neutral event for Japanese equities overall. We expect bank stocks to undergo correction for time being, despite rising inflation expectations Also, if oil prices remain elevated they could push up long-term rates by way of increased inflation expectations. Rising long-term rates are typically an upside driver for bank stocks, but we do not think strong bank stock performance will necessarily result from rising long-term rates/inflation expectations in the absence of a change in BoJ monetary policy. Core PCE inflation has printed back -to- back 0.4% monthly prints, lifting the year -over-year rate to 3.1% -- its highest since early 2024 – and we are tracking a third consecutive 0.4% print for core PCE in February. The ongoing oil price shock will significantly lift headline inflation. The key will be how officials interpret any passthrough to core prices. No doubt Powell will aim to treat this as another adverse supply shock that the Fed should look through if they are able. Here he will emphasize the need to keep inflation expectations stable. But it is also worth noting that Fed staff modeling leads to different conclusions about the extent of this passthrough, with FRBUS suggesting an oil price shock can lower core inflation through the aggregate demand channel (see here), while other work focused on the 2022 energy price spike concludes it could lift core inflation for a sustained period (see here). With inflation still well above target, it makes sense for another supply shock to argue for some caution in easing policy imminently. Amongst other topics, we expect Powell to be quizzed on the potential effects of AI on the economy – a topic that dominated market attention prior to the events in the Middle East. In addition, several countries have already announced ‘ad hoc’ support—for example, South Korea will cap retail fuel prices as of the level at end-February, effective today (March 13), and review these caps every two weeks going forward. This arguably marks the most significant intervention by the Korean government in fuel markets since deregulation nearly three decades ago. Given these actions, fiscal policy is likely to ease in the majority of regional economies as a result of the oil shock. Of course, subsidy spending could be offset by cuts in other areas, but we suspect in most cases the result is likely to be a net loosening. This adds to pre-existing pressures to boost domestic demand: much of the region was already facing a more challenging export environment due to US tariffs and intense competition from Chinese manufacturers. The implications of the energy shock for monetary policy are mixed, with higher inflation and lower growth pointing in different directions. records.text: Deterioration in regional current account positions To estimate the sensitivity of external balances to higher energy prices, we perform a simple ‘mechanical’ calculation of the net export position multiplied by the price change, for both natural gas (we assume +30%) and crude oil (+20%). This may miss some additional energy price effects on other exports and imports (e.g., thermal coal in Australia); it also does not reflect lags in contract pricing for LNG for example. For this reason, our forecast changes are not always identical to the simple mechanical estimates. The Asia-Pacific economies we cover regularly are all net oil importers. However, Malaysia and Australia are significant natural gas exporters, Indonesia to a smaller degree, so those three economies see current account improvement from higher gas prices. Most of the region are material net importers, with Korea, Thailand, and Taiwan most ‘net short’ from this perspective (Exhibit 10). records.text: 13 March 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 importance than before for the MPC to contemplate further rate cuts. Why November for the next rate cut? Our judgement for some time has been that the median voter's estimate of nominal neutral errs closer to 3.25%. Therefore, the next and likely final rate cut – in our view – will be symbolically important. In delivering such a cut, the MPC will want to see evidence that rising inflation expectations aren't translating to second-round effects and higher wage settlements. We won't have much information on both until Q4-26. Risks to our call are tilting one way at this stage: to one or no further rate cuts this year. Indeed, should the energy shock result in a large and sustained increase in price pressures, the MPC may be minded to put any further rate cuts on the back burner. This could see terminal rate expectations for the MPC rise. What's the dovish risk? The labour market continues to deteriorate, prompting further easing to mitigate against rising slack and an expanding negative output gap. In such a scenario, the MPC could start to overweight downside risks to the economic and labour market outlooks, looking past the energy shock in CPI. records.text: To estimate the impact of the war on the US economy, we rely on a few rules of thumb. On inflation, our rule of thumb is that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices boosts headline and core PCE inflation by 0.2pp and 0.04pp, respectively. On growth, our rule of thumb is that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices lowers GDP growth by 0.1pp without a domestic energy capex response—if, for example, domestic producers are unsure of when the conflict will end and consequently how long prices will stay high—or about 0.07pp with a response. The growth impact from a temporary price increase that gradually fades, as envisaged by our strategists, is roughly half as large. The growth hit from tighter financial conditions—we estimate that every 1pp tightening in our FCI reduces GDP growth by about 1pp over the following year—would add to the effect of higher oil prices. Lessons from Past Geopolitical Events To dig deeper, we look back at the effects of past conflicts on markets and the economy. We draw three conclusions. First, while conflicts have sometimes led to large spikes in oil prices that lasted for a while, their impact on financial conditions has usually been more limited and briefer. The left side of Exhibit 3 shows that oil prices quadrupled after the OPEC oil embargo in 1973-1974 and doubled during the Gulf War. That said, the economy’s exposure to oil shocks is lower today, both because the oil intensity of US GDP has fallen sharply—as shown on the right side of Exhibit 3—

M Idea 2 Gas Our commodity strategists expect a one-month Qatari LNG outage due to a prolonged restart timeline following shutdown last week. This fully removes the LNG market surplus modelled for 2026. Risk to summer storage fill in Europe is contained in a one-month outage scenario, although TTF will still need to price more competitively to attract LNG back to Europe over summer – MS average summer price forecast is €60/MWh, 30% upside to the TTF forward curve. We note that no LNG tankers have exited the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) so far. See The European Gas Manual: Summer Refill Risk (12 Mar 2026). Oil The Strait of Hormuz – through which roughly 20 mb/d of crude and refined products normally flows – has been effectively closed since the start of the conflict. Our commodity strategists estimate that six tankers exited the Strait on 11 March, which includes 1 LPG tanker, vs ~35 normally. With Asian refiners amongst the most exposed to barrels that originate behind the SoH, some are slowing operations as crude availability tightens; this has tightened product supply, and jet fuel prices have spiked in response. On the Upstream side, Martijn Rats has laid out three scenarios, which depend on the pace at which flows through the SoH resume: 1) Flows resume quickly (days not weeks). Brent can remain in the $80–90/bbl range, and if the pre-existing surplus reasserts itself, prices can cool back toward levels consistent with a well-supplied 2026. 2) Flows return, but only partially.

Chair Powell's press conference: Our economists expect Powell to convey a message that the risk to monetary policy is asymmetric. The Fed is more likely to delay cuts — or cut more when it does — than it will move to rate hikes. The dots: Our economists expect the Fed retains forward guidance via the dot plot that indicate it looks to cut rates by 25bp this year and 25bp next year to a terminal fed funds target range of 3.00-3.25%. We think these three factors carry potential to surprise a market that has increasingly assigned lower odds to rate cuts this year. A More Uncertain Path Ahead The economic outlook—and the path for Bank Rate—depends importantly on the evolution of energy prices. Given high uncertainty around the war in Iran, we set out several scenarios (Exhibits 2 and 3). In our baseline forecast—where disruption of the Strait of Hormuz ends after 21 days and energy prices subsequently normalise—we expect 1% Q4/Q4 growth this year (down from 1.5% before the conflict), unemployment at 5.5% (vs 5.3% before), headline inflation at 2.7% by 2026Q3 (vs 2.2%) and slightly higher core inflation (up 0.2pp). We would look for slightly lower growth and somewhat higher inflation in our adverse scenario, where the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted for 30 days and energy prices rise further. We estimate that the outlook would change more substantially with a 60-day disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, which would push oil prices to $150/bbl and imply a slow normalisation of energy prices. In this case, we would expect Q4/Q4 growth to fall to 0.7%, the unemployment rate to rise to 5.7% and headline inflation to peak at 3.5%. We would, moreover, look for materially higher passthrough into pay growth and underlying inflation in this scenario, with core inflation peaking at 2.8% by the end of 2026. There are multiple channels through which the direct involvement of the country in the hostilities affects activity. First, even if most missiles are intercepted, the threat alone has a meaningful impact on supply, as it is considerably more difficult to produce goods and services when workers must regularly seek shelter. In sizing that impact we use the experience from last year when the 12-day military conflict with Iran in June was followed by a 4.5% annualised decline in GDP in Q2, driven largely by this channel. Second, the conflict will also likely lead to a tighter labour market. There has been a large-scale mobilisation in Israel, with 100,000 reservists called up, in addition to the 50,000 currently on active duty. This will likely tighten Israel’s already strained labour supply – a constraint that has weighed on GDP growth since October 7, 2023. Third, the military conflict and the associated uncertainty are also likely to dampen (both domestic and external) demand for goods and services, with the exception of defence expenditure. Finally, both the disruption to Israel’s gas sector and higher global oil prices are likely to exert a negative impact on overall economic activity. This historical analogy has, unfortunately, sharpened: the ongoing Iran war echoes the 1990/91 Gulf War. As in the early 1990s, the surge in energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty is poised to counteract the growth impulse from a large-scale fiscal expansion. It will weigh on Germany's trade balance, dampen consumer spending, and exacerbate existing competitiveness challenges for German industry. The situation on the ground and in global energy markets remains highly fluid and volatile. At the time of writing, markets are pricing a scenario far from the magnitude and duration of the 2022 energy price shock. Nonetheless, even a milder and more transient shock than four years ago is likely to meaningfully delay Germany's recovery, especially given the already lackluster start to the year. Beyond the direct costs of higher energy prices, the Iran war has reignited uncertainty and tightened financial conditions just as global trade tensions appeared to be receding. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 0.75% in December and kept it unchanged at the most recent January meeting. We expect the bank to maintain its current policy stance again at this meeting. Consistent with this view, none of the 51 BoJ watchers surveyed by Bloomberg expects a rate hike in March. We anticipate that the BoJ will move toward a rate hike in April, after reassessing economic conditions through indicators such as the Tankan survey and the branch managers’ meeting. April is also the most frequently cited timing for the next rate hike among BoJ watchers (April: 37%, June: 22%, July: 29%; Figure 1). Impact of oil and currency on BoJ policy As Governor Ueda has previously noted, a surge in crude oil prices entails two-sided risks on underlying inflation. On the one hand, higher oil prices could weigh on underlying inflation through a weakened economic activity; on the other hand, they could push up underlying inflation via a rise in medium- to long-term inflation expectations. As a result, oil price shocks increase the likelihood of both a rate hike and a policy hold. records.text: M Update 2 February CPI CPI came in below our expectations, with core prices rising 0.22% m/m in February (MS: 0.27%, consensus: 0.20%) and headline prices up 0.27% m/m (MS: 0.32%). As a result, core CPI stands at 2.47% y/y and headline CPI at 2.43% y/y. Based on this print, we revised up our February core PCE inflation forecast to 0.42% m/m, from 0.27% prior to the CPI release. The upward revision is driven by core goods PCE inflation, which we now track at 0.85% m/m—well above core goods CPI. This divergence reflects differences in CPI versus PCE weights, with goods carrying a higher weight in PCE posting sharp price increases. Combining the updated February estimate with our January core PCE forecast of 0.50% m/m implies a steep sequential acceleration in 1Q26, broadly in line with our expectations. We now estimate the 3 month and 6 month annualized rates of core PCE inflation at 5.24% and 3.81% in February, respectively (up from 3.07% and 2.87% in December), while the 12 month pace rises to 3.16% from 3.00%. For the Fed, the sharp increase in prices early in the year is not new information, as policymakers are well aware of the typical strength in core inflation in January. That said, the momentum in core inflation, combined with a potential boost to headline inflation from oil prices, could delay the rate cuts we currently expect later this year. records.text: M Idea 2 Introduction Japan’s equity market remains a cornerstone of global investing, offering a mix of globally competitive technology, industrial, financial, and consumer franchises. This report tracks how institutional mutual fund managers are positioning within Japan, where capital is concentrated, how exposures compare to benchmark weights, and how these stances are evolving over time. This edition of our Fund Navigator: Positioning in Japan Equities draws on fund portfolio observations with a snapshot date of end-January 2026, available as of March 10, 2026. The dataset covers 381 Japan Equity funds with $110bn in TOPIX 500 constituents, and 4,287 Global Equity funds with $285bn in Japanese equity holdings drawn from their broader portfolios. Relative to expected disclosures, coverage rates of Japan funds reached 52% for January, 33% for December, and 72% for November, while those of Global funds were 50%, 56%, and 77%, respectively, providing a representative sample of institutional positioning. To address the reporting lag inherent in fund disclosures, we extend each fund’s most recent snapshot forward and adjust for subsequent market returns. This refinement ensures continuity of positioning estimates between reporting dates, while retaining consistency with reported holdings. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 13 March 2026 Citi Research 3 The Japanese government has made the decision to release oil reserves and reinstate subsidies to keep the price of gasoline to around ¥170/l. Big petroleum wholesalers have raised the price they charge retailers for gasoline by around ¥26/l, so Middle East tensions are starting to have a direct impact on households. This is necessary policy action in societal terms and should limit prices in the near term. Subsidies will initially be paid from the ¥280bn remaining in the established fund, and if needed funds will likely be allocated from reserves next fiscal year. The IEA’s decision to release reserves will compensate for around four weeks of the supply that usually passes through the Strait of Hormuz and should also help limit upside for prices. Our Commodities Team forecasts a core range of $80/bbl–$100/bbl for Brent crude over the next two weeks, but prices have already risen above that range. The risk is that prices continue to decline if the conflict continues for an extended period. That would cause an increase in the fiscal burden for the government to maintain the ¥170/l cap. Electricity prices will also rise, and the government is likely to consider policy action to limit them also. This could also bring forward the restarting of nuclear power generation capacity. While these policy measures are possible, there could be a cessation of supply for other items. In some cases a force majeure has effectively been declared.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley MUFG 17 Data Appendix Data Coverage Research based on fund positioning data faces structural constraints: holdings disclosed by fund management companies are subject to a reporting lag, typically spanning one to two months between the portfolio snapshot date and the point when the data become publicly available. In addition, funds report their holdings at different cadences, some monthly, others quarterly or semi-annually, and a smaller group annually. The result is an uneven flow of data that can complicate aggregation and may affect the immediacy of insights. To ensure transparency and enhance the usefulness of our findings, the exhibits in this section outline how the data are sourced and processed, and summarize data availability at the time of publication. Two structural features of the dataset stand out. First, pronounced spikes in March, June, September, and December reflect the quarterly disclosure cycle, confirming that the quieter months in between are mechanical lulls rather than true gaps in coverage. Second, the underlying trend has been gradually upward over time as new vehicles enter the sample. Taken together, these patterns provide reassurance that the empirical base for this analysis is both broad and steadily expanding. To reduce the artificial swings caused by these staggered reporting cadences, each fund’s most recent holdings are carried forward and adjusted for intervening market returns until a new snapshot becomes available. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 oil price shocks, but we think it is a useful reminder since this is likely the message FOMC members will receive from staff during the March meeting. Optimal policy says the Fed should largely ignore any oil-driven increase in inflation since higher oil prices tend to raise headline inflation but not core inflation. This result arises from several sources. First, by definition, headline inflation includes energy prices while they are excluded from core inflation. Energy directly enters the consumer's consumption basket through gasoline, home heating oil, jet fuel, electricity, among other items. Second- round effects are needed to transfer higher energy costs into other prices. For second-round effects on core inflation to arise, it would have to come through other marginal costs like labor, product markups, or inflation expectations. This normally does not happen because higher oil prices act as a tax on real income and spending power, reducing aggregate demand and limiting firm pricing power. In addition, the shift in the US economy from goods production to services providing means the economy is less exposed to energy costs than it was in prior decades. Finally, the Fed benefits from established credibility on inflation, resulting in low and stable inflation expectations, even through recent inflation experience. records.text: e energy supply shock is something a central bank can 'look through', conditional on core/underlying inflation remaining at target and inflation expectations remaining anchored. The look-through strategy might only be appropriate if the shock is temporary and/or moderate. To gauge the need for monetary policy to tighten in response to rising energy costs the ECB will be thinking about the following: First, whether the inflation projections show a sufficiently large and sustained overshoot of the 2% target. A necessary but not sufficient condition to hike would be HICP inflation exceeding the target by at least a couple of tenths in 2026 and 2027 and remaining above target in 2028. Second, whether underlying inflation – core inflation in general and domestic inflation indicators like wage and services inflation in particular – and inflation expectations confirm that upside/overshooting risks are rising. Third, whether financial conditions tighten enough in response to the shock to lean against upside inflation risks. Bear in mind, in 2022 policy rates were negative. During this period there ha ve been equally significant moves in yield components across the term structure . For instance, rising 2y yields were driven almost exclusively by breakevens, while 10 y yields are higher due to rising real yields and breakevens. Although these contrasting contributors hint at current global macro themes, the overall changes ultimately share similarities to prior oil shock analogues. The most useful is 2008 in our view, which had a mild curve steepening, with longer yields responding to a mixture of higher reals and breaks. The ability to use 2022 as a proxy is challenged given that yields were already at historically low levels, which led to extremes for both reals and breaks going into that oil shock. So, while the recent rise in longer real yields shows moderate underperformance, we don’t find that to be a compelling reason to short duration, particularly given continued AI driven growth concern s along with weakening employment metrics. What is notable is the 2 - way price action today (daily gyrations to both higher and lower levels), relative to the 2008 analogue, which was more one way in nature. We expect the MPC to keep Bank Rate steady at 3.75%. Put simply, the MPC won't be in any rush to cut Bank Rate. The vote split. Six weeks ago, the MPC was finely divided. Four members opted for an imminent rate cut. We now think the March decision will come with a less divided MPC. We expect seven members to vote for a hold in Bank Rate. And we expect two members to vote for a rate cut (Dhingra and Taylor). Why the change for Breeden and Ramsden? Before the energy price rise, the cut in March was a fairly likely scenario in our view. But the recent energy price rise is likely to mean the BoE is in wait and see mode to get clarity next week and monitor how sustained and large the energy price shock is. The BoE has become increasingly sensitive to energy price moves, especially as second round effects to inflation and wage expectations from energy moves have become more prominent in the last few years. We delay cuts to June/September Assuming energy price moves reverse in the next couple of months and we don’t get a protracted conflict, we expect two cuts in June and September (vs March/June before). We still see a path for further cuts, if energy price moves reverse, energy price shock is relatively short-lived and doesn’t increase inflation expectations materially. Rates are still restrictive, disinflationary Budget measures kick in in April, wage growth is easing, risks to growth are on the downside and the labour market is much weaker compared to the 2022 energy shock. Catalyst.Metric: Energy prices pass-through to core inflation

records.text: The monetary policy implications of the ongoing spike in energy prices depend n importantly on whether the shock creates second-round effects in underlying inflation. A key insight from the 2022 episode is that the risk of such pass-through effects depends on the size and persistence of the energy shock, but also the economic conditions at the time. Comparing the current energy shock with 2022 shows that (so far) it is n significantly smaller, narrower and expected to be less persistent. The Euro area unemployment rate is lower than in 2022, but alternative indicators (including vacancies) point to a looser labour market. While core inflation remains above target in the Euro area, it is notably lower than in January 2022. Fiscal and monetary policy is less expansionary now than in 2022 and the current shock looks more global in nature given the large increase in oil prices. We estimate a Euro area cross-country panel model to quantify the potential n second-round effects from non-core (food and energy) prices to core inflation in the current circumstances. We find that pass-through is limited for most commodity shocks, suggesting that second-round effects are negligible during normal times. But our estimates show that pass-through is non-linear and state-dependent, pointing to significant second-round effects in response to large shocks in a strong economy (measured with a tighter labour market and looser fiscal policy). BoE preview: March no more, may be June if all goes well We change our BoE call from a cut to a hold in March, given the recent rise in energy prices. The recent energy price surge means the BoE is likely to be in wait and see mode next week to get clarity and monitor the duration and size of the shock. We expect a 7-2 vote in favour of a hold in March, with risks for 6-3. We expect the BoE to keep its easing bias but add that recent geopolitical events have increased uncertainty around inflation and the bank rate. It is likely to emphasize that the bar for hikes is high. Assuming energy price moves reverse in the next couple of months, meaning the shock is relatively short-lived and doesn’t increase inflation expectations materially, we would expect two cuts in June and September for now (vs March/June before). But this is a low conviction call. We see significant risks and uncertainty around inflation and the BoE’s rate path, depending on the length of the conflict and energy price moves. We could see an earlier cut in April if energy price moves reverse in the next few weeks, or further delays and fewer cuts this year if the conflict is prolonged. If the moves are sustained for much longer or become larger with the conflict continuing into Q2, it can add to doubts on whether the BoE can cut twice this year with one cut potentially more likely.

records.text: UBS Core PCE prices increase 0.36%, 12-month inflation edges up to 3.1% Headline PCE prices (the FOMC's official inflation yardstick) rose 0.28% in January — a surprisingly large 6bp below our 0.34% expectation. The 0.28% increase was a little below the 0.36% increase in December and the 0.35% increase in January of last year, but, nonetheless, was one of the stronger increases of the past year. With today's release 12-month PCE price inflation fell to 2.83% through January from the 2.90% through February in published in the most recent release prior to today. We expect PCE price inflation, which has risen about 0.6pp since April of last year, to increase around another 0.7pp by the second quarter of this year to a 12-month inflation of around 3.6%. The additional pick up is largely a result of rising oil prices, but also some increases in core PCE price inflation. Core PCE prices rose 0.36% in January — 0.07pp below our expectation (0.43%). The 0.36% increase was in line with the 0.36% increase in December and above the 0.31% increase in January last year. As a result 12-month core PCE price inflation rose to 3.1% (3.06%) its highest level since February 2024 and is up ½ pp from 2.6% in April of last year. The reason for our error was the BEA's assessment of legal services prices, and assuming a moderate change than the CPI source data suggested. Given that the global economy and its oil dependency have definitively changed over the past three decades, it is more sensible to compare the current shock to the Ukraine/Russia war than to the 1990 Gulf War. Although the pattern of the shock is similar, the starting point and levels are significantly different. Before the start of the Iranian shock, oil was at USD 60/bbl; in 2022, it was above USD 90/ bbl (Figure 2). Gas shows a similar picture (Figure 3 and Figure 4), with the shock following relatively closely what happened in 2022, but the levels being significantly lower now than in 2022. At the end of last week we published a note evaluating the economic implications of two distinct scenarios. The first projected oil and gas prices at levels observed on the morning of Friday March 6th (oil at approximately USD 85/bbl and gas at EUR 50/MWh). The second envisioned a more severe situation, with oil at USD 120/bbl and gas at EUR 75/ MWh. By Monday, March 9th, intra-day oil prices suggested we were approaching the second scenario. However, by Tuesday, following President Trump's declaration that military intervention might soon conclude, market conditions shifted back largely to Scenario 1. This rapid fluctuation underscores the current market stress and how quickly conditions can change. In our first scenario, Euro Area growth would experience only a marginal impact, with GDP growth decreasing by 0.3 pp relative to our current projections. Given the economy's strong momentum entering 2026, such a shock would be manageable, and we would not anticipate any significant policy interventions. However, the situation could be considerably different under Scenario 2. With oil at USD 120/bbl, we foresee GDP growth being 0.7 pp softer. records.text: The baseline outlook for US equities remains constructive, but the war in Iran n adds to the downside risk posed by elevated valuations. The 5% S&P 500 decline from its January high has continued to follow the historical average equity market path following geopolitical risk events. Our baseline expectation is that the market will eventually resume its upward climb, continuing that historical pattern. However, the outlook now embeds higher oil prices, weaker US GDP growth, and later Fed easing than we and the market previously expected. While the distribution of potential outcomes is wide, the macro headwinds in our base case outlook generally appear priced, the fundamental engine of earnings growth continues to run, and valuations — while still elevated relative to history — are less demanding than they were a few months ago. For corporate earnings, the AI investment boom should offset the drag from n modestly weaker economic activity. Recent earnings reports have reflected the ongoing strength of earnings resulting from AI investment spending, which we estimate will contribute roughly 1/3 of S&P 500 earnings growth this year. In addition, S&P 500 EPS in 2025 realized $275, modestly above our forecast. As a result, we maintain our forecasts for 12% EPS growth in 2026 ($309) and 10% growth in 2027 ($342), but those growth rates now point to a slightly higher level of earnings. records.text: 13 March 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 Lessons in relation to the ECB The stability of inflation expectations cannot be taken for granted. Large and persistent shocks have the potential to de-anchor inflation expectations. The experiences of 2022 and 2008 show how energy prices in particular can lead to a large and rapid shift in the distribution of inflation expectations. The shift in the distribution of inflation expectations can pose a threat to price stability. This risk is something that the ECB is well aware of, and is actively monitoring. Schnabel's speech and recent comments from the Governing Council highlight the focus the ECB is putting on inflation expectations. But that does not necessarily mean that the ECB will be quick to respond. The first part of the ECB's reaction references basing interest rate decisions on "the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data". Given the recent volatility of energy prices, it is likely that the ECB will want to wait and see more evidence in the data of how inflation expectations and economic activity are being impacted before they react. Inflation expectation data is only available periodically. If the ECB is significantly concerned about inflation expectations de-anchoring, and are following a data- dependent approach, this may influence the timing of their policy response. China’s NPC stresses coordination of computing power and electricity: The government work report presented at the NPC (National People’s Congress) on 5 March 2026, for the first time, includes the ‘coordination of computing power and electricity’ as a new- infrastructure project, while outlining the goal of ‘creating a new form of intelligent economy’ (See link, in Chinese). This means the massive electricity needs of AI data centers open up a fresh avenue for soaking up renewable power, driving up demands for power grid upgrade. In fact, China’s robust power supply serves as a strategic advantage for its AI development. According to AI hosting platform OpenRouter’s data, in February, Chinese open- source AI models have topped global token usage, displacing their US counterparts who had dominated the rankings over the past year (See link). The low cost of Chinese AI tokens can be underpinned by the country’s abundant, stable, and inexpensive electricity. China will continue ramping up investment in its power infrastructure to solidify its competitive edge. For example, the State Grid’s investment is expected to reach RMB4trn during the 15th Five-Year Plan, hitting record high and rising 40% from previous five-year period (See link, in Chinese). We Cut Our 2026 Real GDP Growth Forecast for Japan by 0.3pp We revise our 2026 and 2027 Japan economic growth forecasts, incorporating the higher commodity price forecasts. We lower our real GDP growth outlook for CY2026 and CY2027 by 0.3pp and 0.1pp, respectively, to 0.5% and 1.1% (previous forecast was 0.8% for 2026 and 1.2% for 2027). By demand component, we lower our consumer spending outlook versus our previous forecast, primarily due to higher inflation. While we expect continued investments to address labor shortages (particularly in software, a key driver of investment), we believe capex overall could be softer, as some investment projects could be postponed due to greater uncertainty as well as higher material prices. Exports are also likely to come under increased downward pressure from a slowdown in overseas economies. However, we continue to expect the Japanese economy, while decelerating from the impact of rising commodity prices, to maintain positive growth under our baseline scenario. This is based on our view that even if Gross Domestic Income (GDI) is suppressed by deterioration in terms of trade, domestic demand will be underpinned by further growth in wages and corporate profits as labor shortages are likely to intensify structurally. Hawkish/dovish scenarios The price action since the start of the month has erased any premium for rate cuts and the market has now firmly flipped to pricing rate hikes on the back of the energy shock. Therefore, one can argue that the set-up going into this meeting is at the (super) hawkish end of the spectrum, with a 25bp hike priced as of the July meeting and a cumulative c. 43 bp of hikes priced for the year. It is clear that the market expects the ECB to keep all options on the table, signal extreme vigilance on price pressures and underscore policy agility to respond to this shock, so as to curtail de-anchoring of inflation expectations. A relatively hawkish scenario would entail clear indications from President Lagarde that the ECB is concerned by the magnitude of the energy shock, and inclined to pivot towards policy tightening in the not-too-distant future. Hawkish messaging would be reinforced if Lagarde places emphasis on potential risks to inflation expectations, echoing the message from Schnabel's recent speech that " The long period of elevated inflation, and the marked rise in the frequency of supply shocks, has left inflation expectations more fragile than in the past" . records.text: Iran and the US Economy The main transmission channel from the war with Iran to the US economy is the price of oil. Our commodity strategists now expect Brent to average $98 in March and April—up 40% from the 2025 average—before falling back to $71 by 2026Q4. In an upside risk scenario where oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted for a total of one month, they estimate that Brent would average $110 in March and April before gradually declining to $76 by 2026Q4. A more extreme upside scenario with a 60-day disruption to flows through the Strait of Hormuz could see prices average $145 in March and April before declining to $93 by 2026Q4. Our financial conditions index (FCI) has also now tightened by about 0.2pp after responding very little on the first day of the conflict (Exhibit 2, left), and the Fed’s Geopolitical Risk Index has risen quickly too and is now four times its average level (Exhibit 2, right). records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 13 March 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The fog of war The most important factor of the Iran war for the global economy is how persistent energy and uncertainty shocks are. Of course, initial conditions also matter. An energy shock would have a bigger impact on Europe and Asia, which are for the most part energy importers, than in the US, which is now less energy dependent. In the US, the shock could get transmitted through wealth effects, if there is a correction in asset prices. Beneath the surface, it is still a story of chokepoints: the US has incentives to increase control of strategic energy supply and advanced chip technology, to counteract China’s dominance in critical minerals and rare earths (see report Iran FAQ: Dire Strait ). Persistence matters more than spikes As we have argued, the most important economic aspect of the war for the global economy is not so much how high energy prices can spike intra-war, but how persistent the energy shock associated with the war can be (see report Iran: A chokepoints story ). Of course, the conduct of the war influences the persistence of the energy shock and the new floor that energy prices as well as the prices of their derivatives can reach. records.text: UK Economics and Rates 13 March 2026 Citi Research 2 We expect the MPC to hold the Bank Rate at 3.75% at the meeting next week. The economics of a near-term hold are straightforward: the disinflationary process that we have previously outlined (see UK Economics and Rates – BoE: Hawks, Headwinds, and Holding Fire for discussion on disinflation, and UK Economics and Rates Strategy – Rate cuts: a matter of when, not if for the underlying dovish bias in the BoE) is much harder to guarantee while a new adverse supply shock is contributing upside risk to inflation. In this environment, given the asymmetric balance of cost around the two eventualities, preserving policy optionality is the more logical path than front-running further easing to mitigate any risk of undershooting. We never expected a March cut, but now also remove April from our call. April, to us, made sense as the logical cut in a “slow and steady” cycle—inflationary pressures were easy; policy measures would mechanically lower CPI growth; and, crucially, it tracked with both BoE communications about the policy rate being on a downward trajectory while also accommodating some of the more hawkish concerns. We now think this logic no longer holds. The spectre of energy-led reflation now hangs over the Bank, and its origin—as a wholly exogenous shock— once more highlights the vulnerability of the UK’s monetary policy regime, which, once more, must consider the possibility (and probability) of suppressing domestic demand

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 Rates Strategy: Enter Long SFIZ6 Fabio Bassanin We expect the BoE to keep the Bank Rate on hold, with a 7–2 vote split. The market fully prices this outcome (rates on hold), so the focus will be predominantly on messaging. In our base case, the Committee should reiterate that monetary policy is being set to ensure CPI inflation returns sustainably to the 2% target over the medium term. Accordingly, if the Committee judged that higher energy inflation could lead to second-round effects, policy would remain restrictive for as long as necessary to prevent this. However, if upside risks associated with energy prices were to subside, or if recent developments were to add to downside risks to medium-term inflation from weaker demand and a loosening labour market, policy restrictiveness would be reduced further. This framing would signal to market participants that upside inflation risks from the energy spike may be sufficient to delay further easing, but that the bar for near-term hikes remains high. That said, we should be mindful that the messaging could lean more hawkish, as our economists note—for instance, if the statement were to suggest that “monetary policy could be adjusted in either direction, depending on how the latest energy price shock impacts the balance of supply and demand in the economy.” If language along these lines were to appear, we and the market would read it hawkishly and as broadly consistent with current market pricing of

records.text: to remain until October 2027. This statement leaves open the risk scenario of early departure (see here). Risk management and contingency Risk management hikes? At the time of writing, the market is pricing about 30bp of hikes in 2026 (pre-conflict, it was pricing about 10bp of cuts). Last year Philip Lane said that policy rates above 2.5% are clearly restrictive and rates below 1.5% are clearly accommodative (here). Where the ECB puts policy rates between those two levels is “a question of cyclical management”. That raises the possibility that if it is nervous about the risk of persistent inflation, the ECB could hike rates to 2.5% for risk management reasons without being “clearly restrictive”. That is, without taking a big risk with growth. Contingency. The path of monetary policy is contingent on the path of energy prices. It's possible the inflation shock looks transitory now and tough talk from the ECB is enough to keep inflation expectations anchored in the coming months. But if gas market supply in particular takes longer to normalise post-conflict, sticky gas prices later this year could see inflation persistence risk build into year-end. The gas forward curve is less downward sloping now than it was a week ago, implying persistence risk is rising. There are different paths to policy tightening. A scenario in which the conflict subsides while maintaining elevated risk premia is unlikely to derail this year’s solid growth outlook, but will raise 2026 global CPI inflation by roughly 0.5%pt from an already ele- vated level. We do not believe that this scenario will generate the rate hikes now anticipated in Europe, as regional growth will prove relatively sensitive to this shock and an energy price shock of this magnitude is unlikely to derail the positive inflation dynamics evident at the start of the year. This assessment for a pause would change if broader pres- sures on commodity prices and transportation costs reignited global goods price inflation. In addition, a scenario in which oil prices moved to $125bbl or higher could trigger embedded asymmetries in central bank reaction functions. The Fed is biased towards offsetting recession risk and would likely tilt dovish if the oil price shock intensified. Previously, we have argued that a dovish policy vs strong growth environment justifies a steep front-end—given we now face the opposite distribution of risks, we expect further front-end flattening risk. Sovereign credit has repriced wider as EUR rates vol increased, although using our valuation framework we estimate the widening is slightly less than implied by the increase in rates vol and shift in macro fundamentals (Exhibit 6). Using the scenario analysis from our European economics team into our macro vol fair value model, we find the current level of spot vol (somewhat lower than last week’s peak) is broadly in line with fundamentals (Exhibit 5); however, the risks are skewed to the upside should the tension between high inflation and weak growth intensify. In this adverse scenario, risks to spreads would increase. To reflect the above, and a more acute and front-loaded increase in macro uncertainty, we revise our end-2026 10y OAT-Bund, BTP-Bund, and Bonos-Bund forecasts to 75bp, 85bp, and 55bp respectively (from 70bp, 75bp and 55bp). The rise in vol also has implications for other carry expressions, with 10s30s steepeners likely requiring a flatter starting point—according to the fundamental shifts discussed above—but also because of the deterioration in vol-adjusted carry. That said, to the extent that stronger terms of trade and investment effects prove more durable, such dynamics reinforce the upside risks to an earlier tightening cycle, consistent with the risk of a first hike being pulled forward into 2026 that we have previously highlighted. Recent BoC communications suggest that the bar for a hike is lower. Before the oil disruption started, Governor Macklem had noted the concerns around how stronger demand in some sectors "may boost inflation by more than weakness elsewhere lowers it". And about a month later, Deputy Governor Kozicki spoke about the BoC's framework, and showed policy responses as allowing for a fair amount of monetary support/look-through when inflation is above target in the excess supply region. She also noted that the persistence of the supply shock matters, but then combined with the view that the real time estimates will be evolving, she noted that "unless we’re sure the effects will be short- lived, the policy response should be larger than when we can be sure". These communications suggest to us that as long as the domestic employment and spending data do not show any sudden, sustained deterioration, the BoC will remain on hold, and if the initial positive effects of the oil disruption show signs of accelerating growth momentum, the BoC would increase the policy rate.

At the time of writing almost half a hike is priced. While there is a probability of that happening, particularly if the market were to assign a significant probability by then, giving the upper hand to the hawks, we think June would be a more likely time for the first hike of what would be a short hiking cycle. Scenarios next week, other than the more pessimistic one, are likely to show a small overshoot even in 2027. This is important because so far, the ECB has been flagging its symmetry and willingness to look through small, brief deviations from target. The case against April is that, by then, there wouldn’t be enough new information to provide more clarity on the persistence of that overshoot. The same case could be made about June. records.text: M Idea 4 If oil prices keep rising, we would expect the risk of demand destruction to rise as well. At some point, investors should assess that risks skew much more toward lower inflation in the future, given the demand destruction that even higher oil prices would cause. • At that inflection point, we would expect the 1y1y inflation swap rate to move lower instead of higher. What should investors do if and when oil reaches that price level? We would suggest going overweight US Treasury duration (between the 3 and 5y maturities) and entering yield curve steepeners. (between the 3y-5y maturities and 30y maturities). At that inflation point, we would see an overweight duration position as attractive and asymmetric. Why? • If oil prices rise further still, presumably the risks skew even more toward demand destruction and lower inflation – putting downward pressure on Treasury yields and steepening pressure on the yield curve. • If oil prices fall, risks of demand destruction may fall, but so too should Treasury yields as lower oil prices put downward pressure on breakeven inflation rates and investors risk appetite puts downward pressure on TIPS real yields. As such, we think investors should pay close attention to the 1y1y US CPI inflation swap rate for clues as to when oil prices skew risks in the direction of demand destruction.

Instead, the market is facing an acute shortage of products— diesel, jet fuel, LPG, and naphtha that cannot be consumed simply because they are not available (Figure 4). • The waterway is not only a crude artery but also a major corridor for LPG, naphtha, and middle distillates like diesel and jet fuel, with roughly 5 mbd of refined products normally transiting the strait. Europe is particularly exposed given its heavy reliance on Middle Eastern distillates following the ban on Russian imports. Since 2023, the region has also become a major jet fuel exporter, aided by the start-up of Kuwait’s export-oriented Al-Zour refinery. • With exports stranded and no pipeline‑rerouting options available, roughly 2 mbd of Middle Eastern refining capacity is effectively offline due to export constraints and infrastructure attacks, tightening global product balances almost immediately. The squeeze is already acute in middle distillates— particularly diesel and jet fuel —given the Gulf’s role as a key supplier to Europe, Africa, and Asia. Our expectations around the Bank of Canada's response Our current call for the Bank of Canada is to remain on hold for the rest of this year and hike in 1Q27. We are of the view that the BoC would need to assess the read-throughs for cyclical inflation, specifically in the context of the excess supply situation that the economy is currently in. The risk to our call is that the BoC hikes sooner, as early as 3Q26, if the oil shock persists. Although the ToTEM framwork suggests a policy hike, we are cautious about using that implication directly here. The current starting point for the Canadian economy is one of excess supply and a softer cyclical backdrop. The ToTEM results that imply increases in the policy rate should be interpreted as deviations from steady state rather than from current conditions. As a result, while a positive oil price shock does provide some uplift to domestic demand through income and wealth channels, and does not meaningfully feed through to core inflation measures, this impulse is insufficient to warrant a near term Bank of Canada hike. Moreover, a larger or more persistent commodity shock would likely weigh on US and global growth, with negative spillovers to Canadian non commodity export demand offsetting some of the domestic gains. Our economists now expect higher inflation to delay Fed and BoE cuts in their baseline, and the distribution of risks for the ECB has also shifted in a hawkish direction. This justifies somewhat higher front-end yields in the near term, although growth risks will likely limit the degree to which yields can rise. Our baseline growth expectations have also been revised lower by around 0.5pp n in major markets, and the downside risks to global growth will only increase with further energy price upside. With looser labor markets and tighter policy rates as a starting point compared to the energy price shock in 2022, we think rates can only go so far before growth effects dominate and yields eventually fall. This suggests the asymmetry is building in rates markets, with the skew of risks towards lower yields. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 13/03/2026 14:05:31 GMT Distributed on: 13/03/2026 14:05:31 GMT 13 March 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe United Kingdom Economics UK Weekly Digest Date With inflation risks now skewed firmly to the upside, and inflation expectations likely to follow suit, one question we've been asked is: what would it take for the Bank of England to hike rates? The simple answer: a lot. In this weekly, we look at why the case for rate hikes – at least for this year – remains weak. We also lay out the conditions for what we would need to see for the BoE to genuinely consider adjusting policy rate higher. This is not 2022 To start with, this is not 2022. Three years ago, the economy was on the rise. GDP growth ramped up by 5.2%. Fiscal policy was loose. Monetary policy was accommodative. Inflation was surging (even before the energy shock). The labour market was tight. Wage expectations were accelerating. And the global economy was in a cyclical upswing. Not to mention, supply chain disruptions had already started to feed through meaningfully into stronger core goods and food inflation. Today, the world has changed. Fiscal policy is tightening rapidly. The UK is set to see the biggest fiscal consolidation (on paper at least) among G7 countries. Monetary policy - though less restrictive than a year or two ago, remains restrictive at 3.75%. Growth has stuttered to a near standstill - with Q4-25 GDP growth barely pushing into positive territory
