A delay to the recovery Even a milder and more transient shock than four years ago is likely to meaningfully delay Germany's recovery. Beyond the direct costs of higher energy prices, the Iran war has reignited uncertainty and tightened financial conditions just as global trade tensions appeared to be receding. Jointly, these effects are likely to shave at least 0.3 percentage points from GDP growth this year. The deterioration in the terms of trade should amount to an at least a 0.1ppt hit to net trade, while the positive growth contributions from private consumption and investment could also each be 0.1ppt lower as a result of rising producer and consumer prices. Headline CPI inflation could rise to over 2.5% this year, with the energy price shock accounting for about 0.5ppts. records.text: Energy prices have been volatile amid the ongoing conflict in and around Iran, as n markets attempt to gauge the length and severity of damage to energy infrastructure and disruption to transit through the Strait of Hormuz. As of this writing, spot Brent crude oil prices are around $100/bbl, a ~40% increase over the past two weeks. The price of natural gas for shipping to Europe and Asia has also surged higher. Alongside these developments, our commodities research team has further n upgraded their oil and natural gas price forecasts in recent days. They now expect Brent crude oil prices to average over $100/bbl in March, $85 in April, and gradually ease back to the low $70s late in the year. Relative to futures prices early in 2026, this represents slightly over 20% increase in the average price over Q2-Q4. The increase in natural gas price forecasts is even larger. Relative to our base case, risks remain skewed to “higher for longer” prices. With this publication we refine our model-based estimates of the effects of these n higher energy price forecasts. We note that the limited sample size of large historical energy supply shocks, and the range of factors that affect growth and inflation, make it hard to pin down growth and inflation effects precisely. And policy actions by governments can cushion the short-term impact of commodity price shocks on the economy. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 12/03/2026 10:12:38 GMT Distributed on: 12/03/2026 10:12:38 GMT 12 March 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe Economics Focus Europe Date Iran shock and the case for fiscal intervention: 2022 vs 2026 Europe is currently confronting a significant shock, with the sudden surge in energy prices echoing the challenges faced by the continent in 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. At that time, Europe responded to the shock by implementing a coordinated and substantial fiscal response to shield households and firms from the impact of higher energy costs. The question is whether a similar fiscal response would or could materialize today. Given the parallels between the current energy shock and the 2022 energy crisis, this note examines the fiscal measures adopted by European governments in 2022 to counteract the crisis. We analyze the scope, nature, and targeting of these fiscal interventions, comparing the situations then and now, and drawing lessons on the conditions under which comparable fiscal support might be deployed again. Public finances are arguably more vulnerable today than in 2022, and growth momentum is weaker compared to the post-COVID reopening phase. However, should households and firms be threatened significantly with an energy crisis that puts the economy on a recessionary trajectory, we believe Member States will intervene. records.text: M Update 2 PCE Inflation: Front-loaded strength this year Core PCE inflation rose 0.36% m/m in January, strong but below our expectation (consensus 0.4%, MSe 0.50%). The range of estimates for this print was wider than usual. In our view, the main source of disagreement among forecasters stemmed from the treatment of two CPI components—legal services and other professional medical services —that feed into core services PCE but were not directly published by the BLS. While it was possible to infer these components using available data, assumptions differed across forecasters. We assumed the BEA would impute these categories using the same methodology it has applied historically. That assumption proved incorrect. Although other professional medical services came in broadly in line with our expectations, legal services was much weaker than anticipated (1.8% m/m versus our 11% m/m forecast), accounting for most of our forecast error. This suggests the BEA applied a more judgmental trend for this category rather than relying on the available CPI information. The January reading is consistent with core PCE 3-month annualized inflation at 3.66% (3.11% in December), and the 6-month annualized pace at 3.13% (2.89% in December). The 12-month comes at 3.06% in January (vs 3.01% in December). The black line shows the “effective” pass-through coefficient from an increase in non-core prices on core prices. records.text: Energy prices have been volatile amid the ongoing conflict in and around Iran, as n markets attempt to gauge the length and severity of damage to energy infrastructure and disruption to transit through the Strait of Hormuz. As of this writing, spot Brent crude oil prices are around $100/bbl, a ~40% increase over the past two weeks. The price of natural gas for shipping to Europe and Asia has also surged higher. Alongside these developments, our commodities research team has further n upgraded their oil and natural gas price forecasts in recent days. They now expect Brent crude oil prices to average over $100/bbl in March, $85 in April, and gradually ease back to the low $70s late in the year. Relative to futures prices early in 2026, this represents slightly over 20% increase in the average price over Q2-Q4. The increase in natural gas price forecasts is even larger. Relative to our base case, risks remain skewed to “higher for longer” prices. With this publication we refine our model-based estimates of the effects of these n higher energy price forecasts. We note that the limited sample size of large historical energy supply shocks, and the range of factors that affect growth and inflation, make it hard to pin down growth and inflation effects precisely. And policy actions by governments can cushion the short-term impact of commodity price shocks on the economy. Using our model-based estimates as a starting point we are revising headline CPI n inflation forecasts up 0.3-1.2p

Growth concerns are likely to linger, but an energy price shock of this magnitude is unlikely to derail the positive core inflation dynamics evident at the start of the year outside the US. There are, however, three developments that could alter our assessment of the likely path for central banks. • Oil spike non-linearity risks reinforce reaction func- tion asymmetries. While oil prices are anticipated to remain elevated, we recognize that closing the Strait of Hormuz for an extended period of time would push prices far above current market expectations. A sustained spike in oil prices to $125bbl or higher would boost inflation and damage growth, but would also increase the risk of non-linearities that could magnify both outcomes. If we move into this space, the asymmetries in central bank reaction functions could be triggered. The Fed is more biased to recession risk and would likely tilt dovish as the oil price shock intensifies. At the same time, the ECB has generally displayed a greater sensitivity to upside infla- tion risk—a development which saw them tighten into energy price pressures in 2008 and 2011, despite clear evidence of building growth risks that ultimately saw the region slide into recession. records.text: Updating our US equity outlook and investment recommendations The headline US equity market has remained remarkably resilient despite another week of geopolitical volatility and rising oil prices. The S&P 500 has declined by 5% from its January high, continuing to trade roughly in line with the average path following other major geopolitical risk events of the last several decades. Conversations with investors have indicated a marked recent increase in uncertainty and pessimism regarding the duration of the military conflict and its implication for equity markets. Nonetheless, most continue to express the view that short-term volatility will eventually give way to a continued upward trend, in line with the historical average pattern. This is also our base case expectation. While the distribution of outcomes following past events has been wide, and limited geopolitical visibility today makes it impossible to rule out the risk of a stagflationary shock, few investors have expressed a desire to dramatically reduce exposure to an equity market that has rebounded quickly from other growth scares during the last few years. While signs of hedging are evident, equity investor positioning generally shows little sign of panic regarding the direction of the market. Our Sentiment Indicator of equity investor positioning is neutral (0.0). With investors generally loathe to sell their portfolios, the options market signals some signs of hedging. records.text: could hike at later dates simply because inflation stay s at elevated levels and does not show signs of returning to target.) First, downside risks to the labor market need to be eliminated. The past two years have shown that the Fed is responsive to weak labor market conditions and downside risks even in the face of elevated inflation. Hikes likely require something more, though . In particular, the labor market likely needs to re -tighten – e.g., with the unemployment rate falling back towards 4%, quits rising, and wages accelerating, among other conditions – and, therefore, return as a source of inflationary pressures. Second, core PCE likely needs to show evidence of accelerating noticeably above 3%. Furthermore, the source of the rise cannot be readily identifiable as a shock that is likely to prove transitory even in the absence of tighter monetary policy (e.g., tarif fs or oil). Of course, there may be thresholds for core inflation where the source of the rise is down-weighted. Nonetheless, to get to hikes the Fed would have to discard a strongly held narrative that a disinflationary trend is in place and that once one -off shocks dissipate inflation will be close to 2%. This would take a compelling story. Clearly, realization of the first point (a re -tightening labor market) would be one reason to reconsider fundamental assumptions about the disinflation trend. The ECB meeting next week will thus be keenly watched to assess how the central bank is inter- preting the impact from energy prices. Our economists think that current spot energy prices and forward curves likely leave the ECB firmly on hold as such an outcome would leave headline inflation in the region at target and core inflation sub-2% in 2H (ECB: Mindful of 2022, but still far from it, Fuzesi). Moreover, parallels to 2022 are not appropriate given key differences: overly easy monetary policy at that time, a post-pandemic demand recovery and other supply constraints. The rate hikes appear excessive and may be one reason why EUR/ USD hasn’t weakened by more but these expectations are misguided in our view. If the ECB were to hike rates amid an energy price shock, it would be adverse for sentiment in the region and the potential downside risks to growth would increase, further weighing on the euro. records.text: Given likely delays in further BoE cuts, we now expect Gilt yields at 4.25% at end-2026 vs 4.0% previously. However, we remain bullish relative to current market prices, and we see dovish risks for the UK curve from current levels. This is because the BoE is more likely to remain on hold in response to higher inflation than to hike. The starting point for the UK labor market is weaker than that in Europe, and increased growth risks would worsen the medium-term outlook for the unemployment rate. Of course, caution around inflation expectations could see the BoE on hold for an extended period in the upside scenarios for commodity prices, but with policy rates more clearly in restrictive territory vs Europe, we think the distribution remains skewed to the downside for UK yields on any deescalation or increased recession risks. Fiscal and political risks will remain a key focus for Gilt investors, and for this reason we have less strong views on curve shape in the UK compared with the flattening we expect in Europe. We think that Gilt risk premium will remain quite directional with front-end pressure, suggesting more parallel yield moves across the curve. For now, we keep our JGB yield forecasts unchanged, and continue to expect 10y JGBs at 2.0% at end-2026. We see two-sided risks around these forecasts. While it is possible the relationship is not directly causal, the relationship is still important enough to consider energy prices as a signal for risks to inflation expectations (whether that risk comes directly from energy prices, or a third-factor that drives both energy prices and inflation expectations). The impact of the 2008 energy shock on inflation expectations 2008 was another episode in which oil prices spiked higher (averaging USD 89 in Q2 2008, up from an average of 55 USD in 2007), while the distribution of inflation expectations also shifted higher (Figure 7).4 In July 2008 (shortly after the oil spike and shift in expectations), the ECB decided to hike rates by a further 25bp after having been on pause at 3% for around a year. At the time, some people questioned the merits of the further hike, especially with the stresses in global financial markets that were starting to become evident (Lehman Brothers would subsequently collapse in September, and the ECB would start cutting rates rapidly in October with a 50bp cut – only 4 months after the additional hike). records.text: Higher Oil Prices: Pre-Shock Disinflation and High Real Rates Reduce Chance of Hikes Following the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz, our commodity team have updated their oil and gas forecasts, assuming in their base case that the Strait will be largely closed for 21 days and only be fully open after a further 28 days. The loss of oil and gas supply will lower inventories to an extent that the impact on prices will likely be felt for a more extended period. The team now see Brent prices averaging US$77/bbl in 2026 and US$71/bbl in 2027 (previously US$71/bbl and US$70/bbl), with oil prices peaking at an average of US$80/bbl in Q2 before declining to US$71/bbl by Q4. Similarly, they expect European gas prices to be about 30% higher in 2026 than previously assumed. Even after this update, the team view the risks to oil and gas prices as skewed to the upside and have provided two risk scenarios that assume that the Strait remains closed for 30 (moderate risk) or 60 (extreme risk) days. In the extreme risk scenario, the team see Brent prices averaging US$105/bbl in 2026, declining to US$93/bbl in 2027. records.text: 13 March 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week ahead ECB policy meeting (Thu) The upcoming ECB meeting on Thursday will be dominated by the recent surge in energy prices and the conflict in the Middle East. We think it is highly unlikely the ECB will change policy at this meeting. Instead, the focus will be on the messaging. We expect the Governing Council to acknowledge the increased uncertainty and the upside risks to near-term inflation, reiterate the flexibility of its current policy stance, and, most importantly, deliver a strong, resolute commitment to maintaining price stability. The key market signal will be the strength of the language used to underline this commitment, which could range from standard phrases to more hawkish "vigilance" rhetoric reminiscent of the Trichet era. Looking ahead, the path of monetary policy is contingent on the evolution of energy prices and the risk of persistent inflation. Our baseline scenario, which holds for now, is for the ECB to keep rates at 2% through 2026 before hiking in mid-2027 as domestic tailwinds begin to dominate. However, the risks are significant. The report outlines two key scenarios: a moderate, transitory energy shock ($80/bbl and gas at EUR50/MWh) that the ECB could 'look through', and a more adverse scenario with a 50% rise in energy costs ($120/bbl and gas at EUR75/MWh) that would likely trigger a recession and a persistent inflation overshoot, forcing a policy response. As such, we also change our call for the terminal rate to 3.25%, with subsequent cuts in June and September. Neutral rate in the UK has always been unclear, and this has been a feature of monetary policy decisions that was likely going to be resolved dynamically as we approached neutral, rather than stated as a preconceived target. Bank communication has always made it clear that a cut raised the bar for the subsequent cut. While we take no strong view on neutral, per se, we had previously argued that a prolonged cutting cycle would necessitate rates dropping lower than market pricing implied on the back of domestic demand weakness. This demand narrative remains, for the most part, intact in the face of surging energy, but the policy implication differs and, in the face of a stagflationary shock, the MPC’s single inflationary mandate removes much of the discussion around a trade-off. We now think that the MPC will settle this round of cuts at 3.25%, with the additional 25bps over our previous call something of a “risk premium” that affords policy space as we approach neutral. That’s especially true given: a) policy rates are already around neutral, b) inflation was expected to undershoot target and the energy moves so far are unlikely to push headline too far above 2% - see European Economics, c) unemployment is rising, d) there is policy error risk of hiking into a potential growth shock, which could be flagged in any scenarios for conflict in the Middle East (see above). The risk-reward to fade the very front-end may look even more attractive given the risk that the ECB meeting provokes an oversized reaction. records.text: James Moberly +44(20)7774-9444 | james.r.moberly@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Sven Jari Stehn +44(20)7774-8061 | jari.stehn@gs.com Goldman Sachs International European Daily: BoE Preview—A Hold Next Week, Delayed Cuts Thereafter 13 March 2026 | 2:43PM GMT Higher energy prices resulting from the war in Iran have increased upside risks to n the UK inflation outlook. We therefore expect the MPC to hold Bank Rate unchanged at next week’s meeting with a 7-2 vote. We expect the Committee to refrain from offering a strong steer on the n near-term policy outlook, noting that in the current context of elevated uncertainty it will decide the appropriate degree of restriction at each meeting. But we think that the guidance will indicate that some further policy easing remains likely if energy prices fall back. We expect that Bailey will convey a similar message in his individual paragraph. The economic outlook and the path for Bank Rate depend importantly on the n evolution of energy prices. LLC Mark Schmidt mark.schmidt1@morganstanley.com +1 212 296-8702 The question of stagflation has come up often among muni investors, who rightly or wrongly see parallels to the 1970s and 1980s in today's oil shock. As our economists note, the moment does not match the mood: • Both the US economy and key state budgets have become more resilient to energy shocks. • Core inflation looks anchored, even if headline inflation remains volatile. • Municipal credit quality remains strong, with a roughly balanced upgrade- downgrade ratio. Month-to-date, the muni index has lost at least 1%. We do not think that price declines are great enough to trigger an outflow cycle. We expect the Fed to reaffirm a dovish bias, which should help retail investor sentiment towards fixed income portfolios. However, we do see the potential for negative excess returns to continue, even if a renewed focus on a softer labor market allows total returns to turn positive once again. There are a few reasons to think the muni curve could prove sticky: • Net supply is rising, and looks likely to stay positive until as late as June. • Long-end munis' continued underperformance could stifle green shoots in fund flows. • Fund flows usually slow around tax time — from late March through mid-April. • Credit spread curves have flattened; any unwind in credit spreads could offset strength in long-end AAAs. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 13/03/2026 07:02:33 GMT Distributed on: 13/03/2026 07:02:33 GMT 13 March 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe Economics Focus Europe Date Jeopardy: Energy prices and the fragility of inflation expectations The current conflict in Iran has once again thrust energy prices into the spotlight, prompting fresh concerns about the potential for another inflationary impulse in the euro area. In a recent speech, ECB Executive Board Member Isabel Schnabel warned that the prolonged peri od of high inflation in 2022-2024 has left expectations more fragile and vulnerable to shocks than in the past. This raises a critical question for policymakers and investors alike: just how sensitive are inflation expectations to swings in energy prices, and what is the risk that they become de- anchored from the central bank's target? To answer this, we analyse two major historical energy shocks: the 2008 oil price spike and the 2022 energy shock following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Our analysis of both the ECB's Survey of Professional Forecasters and our proprietary dbDataInsights household survey reveals a strong correlation between changes in energy prices and shifts in the distribution of inflation expectations. In both episodes, the distribution of long-term inflation expectations began shifting significantly higher at almost the same time as energy prices started to rise and headline inflation breached the 2% level. The appendix shows the details of our model. We start by estimating a simple specification where the pass-through is linear, which implies that the effect on core prices is proportional to the magnitude of increase in non-core prices (grey line in Exhibit 5, left). After that, we estimate a specification where the pass-through is non-linear, which entails the effect on core prices being more than proportional to the increase in non-core prices (dark blue line). Finally, we estimate a specification where the pass-through is non-linear and state-dependent, which means that a tighter labour market and looser fiscal policy can further amplify the effect of a non-core price increase on core prices (red line). records.text: April 26-27, 2011 FOMC meeting reveals then-Chair Ben Bernanke arguing against higher oil prices causing generalized inflation. At the time, supply disruptions following the Arab Spring and civil war in Libya pushed oil prices higher. Bernanke said a “remarkably large amount” of the inflation increase was attributable to oil. He added that there was “a good chance” the increase would be temporary and that oil by itself explained much of the pickup in headline PCE inflation. He then stressed that the relevant policy question was whether the stance of policy was appropriate for the economy, not whether policy looked “easy” in the abstract against higher inflation. To our eyes, this is about as close as a Fed chair can come to explicitly arguing against raising rates just because headline inflation was being pushed up by energy. At the time, the Fed's policy rate was at the effective lower bound and the Fed was continuing to expand its securities holdings. With the Iran conflict, the ECB and the euro area once again find themselves on the receiving end of an exogenous energy (price) shock that has tightened financial conditions. Even though the broader macro setting (ie, supply chain bottle-necks, COVID fiscal stimulus, re-opening demand surge) is quite different from what was seen in 2022, the market has been quick to draw parallels with that time-period with respect to the ECB's reaction function. Understandably, the thinking, or rather the fear, in the market is that 2022's experience may make the ECB adjust policy rates sooner, to ensure that the high-inflation episode is not repeated. After all, Ms. Lagarde has stated that her greatest regret from the previous episode was being bound by forward guidance (of not raising interest rates before ending asset purchases) and that she should have been bolder. Interestingly, in the aforementioned ECB working paper responding to the criticism of a potential delay in adjusting monetary policy, ECB staff find that even with an earlier tightening of policy, inflation would have still peaked at c.8.5% (instead of 10%) but would have resulted in substantial output losses (c.3.6pp relative to its realised path). 12 March 2026 24 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Nowhere to hide

Based on the likely timing of the surveys, it is possible that the Governing Council have some idea of the impact of the conflict on inflation expectations at the time of the April meeting. n CES household expectations: The CES is typically collected from the first Thursday of the month to the first Tuesday of the following month. The ECB reports that typically 70% of their respondents complete the survey in the first 10 days of the collection period. As a result, the next release of the CES data (covering the month of February), which is scheduled to be released on 27 March, will be unlikely to show any significant effect from the Iran conflict – assuming the survey stayed open for the whole window, the Iran conflict would only have affected the last 3-4 days. Instead, it will be the March survey (conducted from 5 March to 7 April) that will give us our first real look at the impact of the Iran conflict on expectations. The first policy meeting at which the Governing Council will have access to this data will be the 29-30 April meeting. The data should be made available to the public shortly after the meeting. n SPF expectations: Based on past survey windows, the exact timing and length of the April SPF sampling window varies significantly. However, the survey is likely to begin in the middle of April (just under 60% of the past surveys have started on 16 April)

Additionally, we find that in times of large energy price rises, companies tend to partially absorb the higher energy input prices rather than fully passing them on to consumers. As Figure 9 shows, this is broadly evident across all Asia nations, where PPI/CPI ratios rise during times when oil prices are rising sharply. Authorities may also intervene in FX markets if moves become extreme and volatility is elevated, which could help curtail compounding effects from a weaker currency on energy-driven inflation. Bank Indonesia has an explicit mandate to maintain FX stability, but we find many others in the region can be similarly interventionist (Figure 10). Markets may also respond to rising inflation risks by raising expectations for rate hikes, designed to help keep inflation anchored, limiting the need for the currency to weaken. However, hikes could weaken growth, making the FX impact somewhat ambiguous. Unless the supply- driven oil-price shock is prolonged, or the output gap is tight though, we think central banks may view resulting inflation as transitory and see no need to respond. records.text: The main transmission channel from the war with Iran to the US economy is the n price of oil. Our commodity strategists now expect Brent to average $98 in March and April—up 40% from the 2025 average—before falling back to $71 by 2026Q4. In an upside risk scenario where oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted for a total of one month, they estimate that Brent would average $110 in March and April before gradually declining to $76 by 2026Q4. Our rules of thumb are that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices boosts n headline and core PCE inflation by 0.2pp and 0.04pp, respectively, while lowering GDP growth by around 0.1pp. The growth impact from a temporary price increase that gradually fades, as envisaged by our strategists, is roughly half as large. To dig deeper, we look back at the impact of past conflicts on markets and the n economy and draw three conclusions. First, while conflicts have sometimes led to large spikes in oil prices that lasted for a while, their impact on financial conditions has usually been more limited and briefer. Second, geopolitical risk also weighs on hiring and investment in ways that extend beyond the effects of higher oil prices and tighter financial conditions. Third, in the recent geopolitical events where the economy slowed the most—the Gulf War and 9/11—the equity market sold off more than in the average event, confidence declined, and oil prices jumped in the first case. Even the most dovish on the MPC, Professors Dhingra and Taylor, could justify such a call as a precautionary measure while the supply shock is assessed. nThe second, and more likely, scenario is a split vote. This could be a 7–2 vote for a hold, or even a 6–3. The exact split matters less than the split itself. The logic here is more complex but important. In this situation, our view is not that we think Profs. Dhingra and Taylor, the most likely dissenters, underestimate the risk of resurgent energy prices but rather opt to keep Bank communication more cognisant of the two-sided risk while also accommodating their pre-shock narrative of underlying disinflation. There are two elements of this. First, as we have noted, a temporary shock presents a fundamentally less hawkish outlook than a prolonged shock. Second, which is related, is that we think the MPC will want to avoid too drastic a shift in tone. Assuming their baseline assumption still holds that rates are on a downward trajectory, then a unanimous vote to hold may send too strong a signal at a time when uncertainty makes such clarity extremely challenging. The net effect, we think, is that the hawkish turn in MPC communications may in fact be less hawkish than it could otherwise be in order to preserve optionality as the shock plays out. records.text: 2 all over again? — Recent price action in energy contracts has, from a central banking perspective, been an unwelcome development. At time of writing, it is not clear that this time around the shock is as bad as it was in 2022, not least because the UK finds itself in a different point in the economic cycle. That said, events are moving quickly, and the narrative could change. How policy responds will be a function of how geopolitical events, and domestic response, play out. Duration is everything — The BoE, we think, has little room to manoeuvre for now, and caution is the appropriate response. In the face of an external energy shock, particularly with the memory of 2022 still fresh, a single-mandate committee has little option but to take a hawkish pivot. For now, uncertainties abound: the duration of the conflict; the scope for pass-through to other areas of the inflation basket; potential fiscal responses. All of these matter for a monetary response, and we think the Bank will remain cautious until the nature of the conflict, and the associated shock, are clearer. Rates Strategy: The market is likely premature to declare easing over — The MPC is much less likely than the ECB to consider near-term insurance hikes, in our view, making BoE pricing to July look elevated. Instead, we expect the MPC to sound cautious but signal optionality to resume cuts later. records.text: rices retrace, some Fed easing this year is likely to be priced back in. The AI concerns may be a different matter. We liken pricing around them to the so- called “peso problem,” which refers to a situation in which an asset’s price embeds a small probability of a large but rare (or unprecedented) event that never materializes. Because the event doesn’t occur in the observed sample, the asset’s expected returns seem too high or low, making what is in fact rational pricing appear systematically wrong. In the current context, whether pricing of a significant AI-driven rise in unemployment is correct or not, it represents a sort of peso problem, and it’s far from clear to us what near-term data or other developments would lead the market to conclude that the risks aren’t as significant as currently perceived. This means cuts priced for next year or beyond may prove persistent even if economic data comes in better than expected. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Economics: Dusting Off the Old Playbook(s) Bruna Skarica In the minutes | The before...: We expect the minutes to be divided into two sections. The first, we think, will outline the state in which the UK economy enters the potential energy price shock. Since the February MPR, inflation expectations have fallen rather sharply, and headline inflation has declined too, although services inflation came in stronger than expected due to volatile factors (namely, Live Music prices). We expect growth will be described as accelerating off a low level from 2H25, and on track to come in a bit below the BoE's February forecast for 1Q26 (0.2%Q vs. 0.3%Q forecast). We also expect to hear something about the flow of spot pay settlements by February, although with a caveat that the sample size is likely to be small. We would assume these are likely coming in line with the Agents' survey from the February MPR (3.4% for 4Q26). ...and after: The December minutes featured a section on the initial estimates of the impact of the November Budget. We expect something similar next week, but applied in the context of the spike in energy prices. Things can move quickly by next Thursday, but as of the time of writing, we think the commodity prices are consistent with the Bank Staff assessing inflation as likely to peak "at around 3%Y" in 2H26. records.text: United States: Inflation Markets A week is a long time in geopolitics We look into how the spike in jet fuel prices might pass through to CPI airline fares. We also preview next week's 10y TIPS auction. Energy prices will go up, then down, but not necessarily in that order The ongoing war between the US/Israel and Iran continues to drive massive volatility in energy prices, and the implications for headline (and potentially core) CPI remain top of mind. Uncertainty is very high, and we are the first to admit a lack of any particular edge on the geopolitical dimension. Much digital ink has been, and continues to be, spilled discussing why the duration of the conflict matters more than any single day's peak, why trade beyond just energy could be disrupted, that US fertilizer imports from the Middle East are large, and yet, there may be wisdom in crowds to retain a base case of expecting a relatively benign macro impact for the US. In trades, we continue to recommend being long both 5y real yields and 5y5y breakevens. Despite the potential near-term inflationary consequences of the war in Iran, 5y real yields remain range-bound, and 1y1y CPI swaps (2.49% at time of writing) are still below their peak (2.55%) from as recently as late January. records.text: Limited Changes to Growth and Inflation Under Base Case, While Rate Cuts Are Delayed Rather than Reversed The shock to oil and gas prices comes at a time when the region is in a relatively benign cyclical and structural position. As we have repeatedly pointed out, the economies are still mostly operating below capacity and expanding below – or, at best, at – trend, while real rates are in most cases still above what we consider neutral levels. Consequently, current account balances are generally healthy, with Romania the main outlier. Reserve levels are higher than historically. That said, we have revised this year’s growth forecasts meaningfully lower, from 2.8% to 1.5%, well below a possibly stale 2.8% consensus expectation. The revision is disproportionately driven by downside changes to GDP in the GCC and Israel, i.e., the countries directly affected by the hostilities. Elsewhere, we think the impact on growth should be more limited. In the CEE, for instance, we have reduced our growth forecast by between 0.3pp and 0.6pp. The outliers are the energy exporters outside the conflict region, but even there we have kept growth forecasts stable rather than raised them. The reason for this is the limited space for them to expand capacity and owing to fiscal rules in some neutralising the impact of the more favourable terms of trade. This forward-filling ensures continuity of positioning estimates between reporting dates, while the formal coverage statistics reported in this appendix remain based solely on actual disclosures. To quantify the real-time disclosure gap across our fund universe, we reconstruct each fund’s reporting rhythm. This process begins by arranging all historical snapshot dates in chronological order and calculating the number of days between each consecutive filing. These intervals are grouped into cadence bands (monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, annual) based on the most recent pattern observed for each fund. Using this cadence classification, we project expected snapshot dates forward for every fund, month by month, through to the most recent month-end. This projection yields a full schedule of fund-month observations that would exist in a scenario with no disclosure lag, allowing us to compute coverage ratios for any given target month-end by comparing expected versus observed filings. These coverage ratios are calculated solely from reported snapshots, even though forward-filling is used elsewhere in the report to provide continuity of positioning between disclosure dates. records.text: We then use the model to simulate pass-through in response to the Iran conflict. We translate our commodity strategists’ baseline and very adverse forecasts for oil and gas prices into non-core consumer prices and—together with our baseline assumptions on the labour market, inflation expectations, and fiscal policy—let the model work out the implications for core inflation. The key feature of our model is that the pass-through from non-core to core prices is estimated, not calibrated, and can vary over time with the magnitude of the shock and the state of the economy. Our model suggests that our baseline assumptions are unlikely to result in large second-round effects in core inflation (dashed blue line in Exhibit 7). But under our very adverse scenario, the pass-through from non-core to core prices would likely increase and lead core inflation to re-accelerate close to 3% (dashed red line). Taken together, our model points to limited pass-through effects unless the energy price shock becomes larger and more persistent. records.text: 13 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Bond Market Strategy Which dislocation to fade in EUR rates The Iran war has led to a significant unwind of two popular trades: long the EUR front end and EUR long-end steepeners. The unwind of these trades has created dislocations that could be tempting to fade. We argue that positioning for higher term premia (beta-hedged steepeners) is the safer option. A long EUR front-end should be hedged with long positions in the back-forwards of commodity curves. Tricky front end A casual overview of ECB monetary policy decisions versus oil prices suggests that the recent spike in energy prices would have historically led to ECB hikes. However, going into the Iran war, HICP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 were slightly below target with downside risks. As a result, the spike in energy prices initially mostly reduced those downside risks. In fact, commodity markets are pricing enough mean reversion for our inflation strategist's updated forecast to still be below target in the second half of next year. As such, if commodity prices are correct, the EUR front end is likely to be overpricing rate hikes this year. Moreover, if fiscal policy is activated to temper the inflationary impact of higher oil prices, the immediate pressure for ECB rate hikes would be further diminished (albeit with greater risks of hikes in outer years). As highlighted in our CPI preview, we were focused on three issues in this release: whether tariff pass through to goods prices is continuing, signs of residual seasonality, and greater clarity on the underlying pace of shelter inflation—a key component of the CPI basket. On tariffs, this print provides strong evidence of ongoing pass through to goods prices. Our decomposition shows a sharp increase in prices for goods more exposed to tariffs. Prices for goods less exposed to tariffs also rose, though that move largely reflects volatility in software inflation and jewelry. Using our January and February PCE forecasts, we estimate that tariffs have lifted the price level by roughly 65bp so far, close to the total effect implied by our models (around 70bp). Following this January–February price reset, we expect core goods inflation to normalize gradually. Post COVID, February has tended to be a strong month for inflation, likely reflecting residual seasonality. As discussed in our preview, much of this seasonality appears to come from “other core services”—core services excluding more predictable components such as shelter, public transportation, education, health care, car insurance, and telephone services. records.text: Monetary policy - though less restrictive than a year or two ago, remains restrictive at 3.75%. Growth has stuttered to a near standstill - with Q4-25 GDP growth barely pushing into positive territory and January GDP unchanged. Crucially, the labour market is in a very different place. The jobless rate has stretched 100bps to 5.2%. Redundancies have spiked. Underemployment has risen to new cyclical highs. Youth unemployment now sits at its highest level since 2015. And there remain few signs that hiring plans are picking back up - particularly with the Middle East conflict likely to cloud the global and domestic outlook. Crucially, inflation expectations are falling. And wage settlements are dropping – with 2026 pay deals a stone's throw away from the Bank's judgement of target-consistent wage growth. Put simply, the UK economy is not in the same place as it was in 2022. The need to rush into rate hikes to curb inflation expectations is small. The trade-offs are more acute. And, while the rise in inflation (and inflation expectations) may curb further rate cuts, the MPC may be more minded to wait on the sidelines as the dust settles on the Iran conflict. However, we think that the sensitivity to oil has declined for a number of reasons. First, the sensitivity of activity to oil price shocks is typically driven by the need for monetary policy to react to the shock. Turkiye’s energy deficit has declined over the years, as has its current account deficit, and hence the need for pro-cyclical tightening is reduced. That said, inflation expectations remain unanchored, implying higher risks of second-round effects that the TCMB would need to contain. Encouragingly, the Treasury has already addressed that risk, with the announcement of countermeasures that should very much limit the impact of the higher Brent prices on prices at the pump. Second, the country has diversified its sources of imports in a way that in our view reduces the sensitivity of Turkiye’s energy import prices to global energy price shocks. The capacity of the gas pipelines from countries with relatively limited alternative outlets that cross Turkiye or end there is larger than Turkiye’s import needs, and gives the country substantial pricing power in gas. For the same reason, they have also raised their forecast for European gas prices by close to 30% for 2026. Even after this update, which assumes that the Strait will remain largely closed for a total of 21 days and then reopen over the next 4 weeks, the team see the risk to energy prices as skewed to the upside, and think that in an extreme risk scenario, in which the Strait is closed for 60 days and only fully open again in 3 months, Brent prices could be as high as US$105/bbl in 2026, declining to US$93/bbl in 2027. Healthy current accounts and reserve levels, as well as high real rate buffers, n should limit the impact of the change to the oil price on the region in the base case of a 21-day closure of the Strait. We generally expect a delay to the rate-cutting cycles that we have been forecasting, rather than central bank hikes. records.text: 3 Insights SPOTLIGHT CHARTS Sentiment hit Not surprisingly the conflict in Iran has triggered a sharp decline in real money risk appetite. Our broadest measure of sentiment – the Behavioural Risk Scorecard (BRS) – fell sharply in recent days from +6 on March 2nd to -4 on March 5th (the latest available data). This is the weakest reading since early December and we need to go back to May 7th to find a weaker sentiment score. Do not forget, the BRS is based upon 20-day flows and so it is not unreasonable to expect the score to fall further in the coming days. And risk positioning is extended Worryingly, the BRS also indicates that real money investors are currently running extended pro-risk positions. The BRS extreme Holdings series currently sits at +7. Generally (and often strongly) positive pro-risk flows since the weeks after Liberation Day have seen institutional investors build extensive pro -risk overweights across asset classes. So much so that the 3m moving average of the BRS Holdings series is now above +6, its strongest reading since 2018. Should the risk-ff sentiment persist, there is plenty of pro-risk positioning to unwind. Rushing back to the USD Talk of the death of the Dollar as a safe haven has been grossly exaggerated. Since the Iran conflict started we have seen real money investors rush back to the USD, with 5-day flows now in the 89th percentile, their strongest reading since early 2024. (March 3) History shows the Fed's response to oil price shocks depends on the economic context. With inflation high, the Fed has focused on inflation; otherwise, it has prioritized growth. Fed models suggest even a large shock would have only a modest impact on growth and core inflation, but the main risk is unanchored inflation expectations, reinforcing a wait-and-see Fed approach for now. Euro area Focus Europe: Iran shock and the case for fiscal intervention: 2022 vs 2026 (March 12) Despite parallels to the 2022 energy crisis, a similar large-scale fiscal intervention today is unlikely without a significant deterioration in the outlook. At current levels, a marked deterioration in regional balance of payments positions seem likely given high energy import penetration. A silver lining, however, is the strong starting point for CEE trade and current account balances prior to the recent flareup in the Middle East (Figure 10). The negative impact on Poland’s current account this year should be around 1.0% of GDP at most in our base case. As such, the deficit could reach 1.6% versus our previous assumption of 0.7%. At face value, this might seem like a high number, but we think it should be balanced against a very strong surplus in the capital account on the back of EU fund inflows. This is still likely to more than offset a current account deficit even in a scenario of elevated energy prices persisting this year. Hungary and Czechia may also record current account deficits this year due to surging energy prices. Unlike Poland, however, any deficits should be relatively small thanks to an outlook for solid surpluses before the Middle East conflict began. We think small deficits are possible for both countries, i.e. no more than 0.5% of GDP. This compares to our previous assumption of surpluses of 1.4% in Hungary and 0.8% in Czechia. records.text: M Idea 6 US GDP tracking: We initiate 1Q tracking at 1.8% Consumer spending, housing starts, durables, and international trade data for January are now reported. They start to sketch out the outlines of real GDP growth at the beginning of the year. The 1.8% pace that we are estimating would be even weaker if not for a rebound in government spending after the federal government shutdown. Private final domestic purchases slow to a 1.5% q/q annual rate, led by the household sector. Real consumer spending, weak in January mostly because of goods prices, rose just 0.1% in November, December, and January. The soft starting point, along with downward revision to 4Q services spending, puts our 1Q consumption estimate at just a 1.6% q/q annual rate. Real goods spending falls at a 1.5% pace as prices continue to hurt purchasing power. Services rise at a 3.1% pace, boosted by electricity usage amid seasonally colder weather. For this reason, when we analyze the impact of crude oil prices on medium- to long-term inflation expectations, we find that even using relatively recent data from a period when inflation expectations were rising, no direct impact is evident, although we note an indirect impact via actual inflation (Exhibit 5). Carter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4703 A rates market ripe for a correction Market-implied Fed policy has changed dramatically in the past two weeks. On February 27, markets had priced the fed funds rate to trough at 2.87%. At present, the market prices the trough rate at 3.30% — a 43bp rise since the conflict in Iran began (see Exhibit 2 ). The two clearest signals in the Treasury market resulting from the US-Iran conflict are: 1. Risk reduction; 2. Upside inflation risks took precedence over downside risks to growth. How long investors choose to view the balance of risks in this manner and the monetary policy guidance from the Fed will ultimately dictate the direction of Treasury yields and the shape of the curve. • But the market-implied trough rate now sits well above where the median FOMC participant deemed long-run neutral appropriate in the latest SEP and just shy of where our economists expect the median end-2026 dot to remain next week. As has been the relationship over the past two years, Treasury yields have followed alongside the rise in the market-implied trough rate (see Exhibit 3 ). records.text: Landscape: Emerging Trends and What's Next (13 Jan 2026). Telcos According to our European Telcos analysts, Telcos are largely shielded from the ongoing geopolitical volatility due to the subscription nature of their business model and minimal exposure to the Middle East. Many Telcos have significantly reduced their international exposure and slimmed down operations to focus on domestic/core markets, although they could potentially be exposed to energy cost spikes. European Telcos are also insulated from AI disruption, particularly to the engineering side of the business. AI exposure could instead be positive through cost savings, AI customer service apps, network management and FTTH roll-out. Ongoing consolidation in the market is another tailwind that could lift pricing power, improve networks and spur innovation. Of the Big Five European Telco markets, the UK has already consolidated, French Telcos continue to negotiate potential deal terms (source: Orange CMD, Feb 2026), and media reports have indicated scope for M&A in each of Spain / Germany / Italy. From a sustainability thematic standpoint, Telcos could also benefit from the rising focus on cyber risk management, with major operators already building out cyber arms to service the Defence industry. Analyst Top Picks: DT, Helios, Swisscom, BT, and Nokia. See Why the European Telco sector can continue to outperform (9 Mar 2026) and Cyber Risk Management – An Overlooked Opportunity? We expect the MPC to cut Bank Rate in June and November, leaving our terminal rate expectations unchanged at 3.25%. The timing of any rate cuts, however, remains highly uncertain. What will determine the scale and pace of rate cuts? First, a resolution of the Iran conflict. A swift reprieve in energy prices we think will almost surely be needed for the MPC to contemplate cuts this year, let alone in the first half of the year. The longer the conflict lasts, the more entrenched price rises will be – for both petrol and gas prices. Equally, the threat of second-round effects will also be pertinent for many on the MPC, including worries of a ratcheting higher in wage settlements. Second, how the labour market evolves from here. Indeed, the labour market is weak. Higher uncertainty could dampen hiring plans even more. The risk of a non- linear kink in the labour market is rising, particularly with HR1 redundancy notifications ticking up in January and vacancies falling further. The Commission activated the GEC in March 2020 after the start of the COVID shock, and the GEC remained in place until 2023. In 2025, the Commission activated the National Escape Clause (NEC) for defense spending for four years until 2028. This allows defence spending alone to increase by 1.5% of GDP and to sustain the increase for four years. Keep in mind that although there is a growing sense of urgency among EU leaders concerning European strategic autonomy, necessitating investments across various sectors, including defense, not all Member States have requested the use of the NEC. Among the "big four," only Germany has requested it. This highlights a significant disparity in fiscal capacity: German public finances can support increased spending, whereas the other large economies face greater constraint. Lesson from 2022: risk of recession needed for a large and coordinated fiscal response The 2022 energy crisis episode shows that, despite high debt levels, Member States did not hesitate to undertake additional measures to support households (largely) and firms. Given tactical considerations, we see the THB as particularly vulnerable in the current environment and remain short the currency via our fiscal risks basket. KEY MESSAGES We outline a framework to assess the sensitivity of EM Asia currencies to supply-driven energy price shocks. Such shocks impact FX via four main channels, in our view: trade balance, inflation, fiscal balance and risk sentiment. The duration of the shock and investor de- risking trends will also have an influence. To assess this, we analyse key metrics, including energy trade balances, FX sensitivity to current account balance shifts, oil reserves, state subsidies and FX risk betas, among others. The THB, KRW and INR appear most exposed in Asia to supply-driven energy price rises, while the MYR, and to a lesser extent the IDR, are the least vulnerable. Analysing price action during previous supply-driven oil shocks, we find USDAsia pairs have broadly not risen as much in this episode as historical betas would imply they should – particularly the THB and IDR. records.text: Lee Ferridge 11 March 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Time to start looking through? KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Calming down? The initial market reaction to higher oil price has been unequivocal: the oil price increase is a pure inflation phenomenon, not a growth concern. On the day prior the to start of the Iran conflict the market was pricing a net 47bp of cuts across the G10 in the next year. On Monday, this pricing totalled 276bp of hikes. This has been pared back a little (to 220bp of hikes) after President Trump hinted on Monday that the war was close to an end. It is impossible to know with any real confidence how long the conflict will last but, with mid-terms on the horizon, we suspect that the US will want a swift resolution. By hinting at this on Monday, President Trump has likely reduced the left-tail risk from markets. Not removed it completely, but at least reduced it. A paper published by Fed staff members modelling the impact of the Russia/Ukraine oil shock found that while it did have a meaningful fairly immediate impact on headline inflation this proved relatively short-lived, while the impact on core inflation and growth was fairly minimal. If that left tail risk of $150 or above oil prices has indeed been reduced (and price action on Tuesday would suggest that it has) then a repeat of this scenario (a short-term pop in headline inflation but little other impact) is rapidly becoming the most likely path

Key Takeaways Core PCE inflation came in strong but softer than our expectation, at 0.36%m/m. Our forecast error is likely explained by a change in methodology this month. Rather than inferring legal services inflation from CPI data, the BEA likely applied a more judgmental trend, biasing the print to the downside. Core inflation continues to accelerate, at 3.1% y/y in January, but we expect deceleration starting in 2Q. Real personal spending rose 0.1% m/m in January. We are tracking 1Q real consumption up 1.6% (q/q saar). Real DPI rose 0.7% m/m, boosted by tax changes. 4Q GDP revised -0.7pp to 0.7%, on softer services. 1Q GDP tracking unaltered at 1.8%—stronger Jan spending, weaker capex, big boost from gov't reopening. We then set out our own stylised Bank Rate paths for our scenarios (Exhibit 5). In our baseline forecast, we see the next rate cut in July, followed by November and February to a terminal rate of 3%. While a cut in April is possible if the energy price spike unwinds quickly, we believe that the MPC is more likely to wait for increased clarity before resuming its rate cuts. We would expect the BoE to delay rate cuts further in the adverse scenario (with the next cut in November) and the very adverse scenario (with the next cut not until 2027H2), but we would not look for a hike given that monetary policy remains restrictive at the current policy rate and the labour market is weakening. records.text: more positive news for the MPC. Inflation outlook more uncertain The recent rise in energy prices could put the Bank’s disinflation path in jeopardy. At current market rates, we would expect headline CPI to be revised up nearly 0.5pp this year, lifting the Bank's projections meaningfully. The rise in CPI will likely be seen as temporary, given the current shape of the gas/oil futures curves. In the medium term, inflation would still be expected to fall – and perhaps fall more quickly than previously envisaged. Falling energy prices further out the curve would squeeze real incomes and demand, putting significant downward pressure on domestically generated inflation – particularly given the current projected output gap. As such, based on current market expectations, the Bank’s CPI projections would likely show a swift return to target CPI by the end of the forecast horizon (including perhaps an undershoot of the 2% target). The big question for the MPC will be around the potential for second-round effects, including a potential ratcheting higher of inflation expectations given the bump in energy prices. We would expect this to add some upward pressure to price momentum while introducing an upward uncertainty skew for some MPC members. records.text: Middle East continues to keep oil prices supported. With uncertainty remaining high, we prefer adding new risk via RV structures. We favour adding short THBKRW exposure here. THB relatively more vulnerable to the energy shock: As discussed in FX: Asia’s sensitivity to supply-driven energy shocks (dated 10 March), we view THB as particularly vulnerable in the current environment. Thailand is one of the largest importers of energy in the region, particularly from the Middle East, and holds low oil reserves. Its fiscal balance is likely to deteriorate due to retail fuel price caps and suspended fuel exports, at a time when public debt levels are already elevated. The conflict may also weigh on tourism receipts with flights to/from and via the Middle East being reduced. Moreover, THB’s sensitivity to changes in its current account balance, and to risk-off market dynamics, leave the currency vulnerable. Our analysis also suggests THB has not weakened as much as historical betas during past supply-driven oil rises would imply, suggesting scope for THB to underperform even if oil prices stabilise here. KRW looks more resilient: While KRW also screens as vulnerable in supply-driven energy shocks (South Korea: Q&A on sensitivity to Middle East tensions, dated 5 March), we view it should fair relatively better than the THB as: ▪ South Korea holds more sufficient oil reserves relative to many peers in the region – the authorities suggest ~7months of oil demand (Korea Times). ▪ They have

We are initiating an MXN - basis payer ( 1 m 9 m) trade . The position aims to capture potentially stronger USD inflows from remittances, while the March - April tax season may curb MXN liquidity ; this mismatch between USD - MXN cash balances should add upside pressure on the short - end basis . At the same time, the reduced MXN long positioning, combined with the risk of further Middle - East escalation, suggests an upside bias for the MXN basis . Stronger USD inflow meets tax seasons : We believe the MXN cross - currency basis could experience a seasonal upside push in March and April due to fresh dollar inflows from larger remittances and increased MXN cash demand from the tax season . Since 2010 , the 1 - year MXN basis has tended to rise on average by about 17 bp (excluding 2020 and 2018 due to data quality issue), as shown in Figure 1 . Historically, March often sees a rise in remittance inflows . This is largely because U . S . economic activity picks up as the weather warms (e . g . , more construction activity), boosting disposable income for Mexican workers in the United States (Figure 2 ) . The seasonal surge in USD inflows via remittances tightens local USD funding and could push the near - end basis lower . Our Granger - causality tests confirm that month - over - month change

For instance, GBPUSD has traded resiliently, despite the UK being an energy importer, because of the sharp repricing in front-end rates. Currencies have therefore been more insulated by front- end rates than in past supply-driven oil shocks. We think this is partly because the market is putting more emphasis on the inflationary implications of the oil shock than the growth implications – and partly because of a positioning washout in the front end of global curves. KEY MESSAGES In this note we answer key questions about the impact on FX of the recent energy price shock. We conclude that FX has reacted less to the recent energy price shock because rate differentials moved against the USD meaning nominal rates insulated currencies, in particular those of energy exporters like EUR, GBP and SEK. We are not convinced this will last. We observe the market typically transitions from focussing on inflation upside to growth downside, based on US real yields and inflation breakevens, around 2-6 weeks after the peak in oil. Each is z-scored and normalised from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates the least risk of reflation and 1 the most risk of reflation. Note that z-scores are computed across our sample of EM countries, rather than one country’s history. As such, a normalised z-score of 1, for example, means the raw data point stands the most standard deviations away from the EM sample mean, rather than the historical mean of that country. Intuitively, each country’s (i) energy trade balance and (ii) average FX move under past supply-side oil shocks, are reverse-normalised (e.g. the more negative a country’s energy trade balance, the higher the risk to experience reflation). We attribute equal weights to each indicator.

She is likely to emphasise that policy is not in a “fixed place” and that the Governing Council is well positioned to respond to the unfolding shock. We would expect Lagarde to reiterate her recent comments that the economy has a better capacity to absorb shocks than in 2022. But we expect her to stress the uncertainty created by the Iran war, noting that Governing Council members are more focused on the upside inflation risks, and that the ECB will monitor any signs of persistence and the implications for the medium-term outlook. That said, we expect Lagarde to note that there is no need to rush into decisions but that the Council will respond to the shock as required to maintain medium-term price stability. We see significant risks around this baseline expectation for the meeting (Exhibit 5). records.text: The Risk of Second-Round Inflation Effects from the Energy Price Surge Our scenario analysis shows that the war in Iran could have major repercussions for European growth and headline inflation via sharply higher energy prices. The implications for monetary policy, however, depend importantly on whether the energy shock creates second-round effects in underlying inflation. The ECB can likely look through the energy shock without such second-round effects as growth and headline inflation move in opposite directions. But the 2022 energy crisis shows that the Governing Council might need to tighten policy if second-round effects emerge. A key insight from the 2022 episode is that the risk of second-round inflation effects is state-contingent. Previous studies—including by ECB staff and ourselves—show that large, broad and persistent commodity shocks are more likely to pass through into underlying inflation. Moreover, second-round effects tend to be more pronounced during stronger economic conditions, including tight labour markets, elevated inflation and expansionary fiscal policy. 2026 vs 2022 To explore the risk of second-round effects in response to the war in Iran, we start by comparing current economic conditions in the Euro area with those in February 2022. First, we explore the size, breadth and persistence of the current energy spike (Exhibit 1). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Third, the February CPI print confirmed continued deceleration in the underlying trend in shelter inflation. We think it is increasingly clear that rent inflation will soften over the rest of 2026. The key question is whether monthly readings fall below the pre COVID trend of 0.26% m/m. After this week’s CPI release, we took some signal and revised down our shelter inflation path to a pace slightly below the pre COVID average, at around 0.24% m/m. Taken together, these three factors point to a near term deceleration in core PCE inflation. Are there risks to this outlook from the recent upswing in oil prices? The main risk would be a potential de anchoring of inflation expectations, but we assign a low probability to that scenario. As we have shown in recent work, if inflation expectations remain well behaved, the effect of oil shocks on core inflation is limited. The FRB/US model implies a near zero impact on core inflation, and our own dynamic estimates suggest roughly 3bp for every 10% increase in oil prices—but only if the oil shock is persistent enough to generate second round effects. For the Fed, we see risks skewed toward later—and potentially more—cuts than in our current forecast (two cuts in June and September this year). Given heightened uncertainty, the Fed may choose to wait for clearer evidence of deceleration in core inflation. records.text: Deterioration in regional current account positions To estimate the sensitivity of external balances to higher energy prices, we perform a simple ‘mechanical’ calculation of the net export position multiplied by the price change, for both natural gas (we assume +30%) and crude oil (+20%). This may miss some additional energy price effects on other exports and imports (e.g., thermal coal in Australia); it also does not reflect lags in contract pricing for LNG for example. For this reason, our forecast changes are not always identical to the simple mechanical estimates. The Asia-Pacific economies we cover regularly are all net oil importers. However, Malaysia and Australia are significant natural gas exporters, Indonesia to a smaller degree, so those three economies see current account improvement from higher gas prices. Most of the region are material net importers, with Korea, Thailand, and Taiwan most ‘net short’ from this perspective (Exhibit 10). Moves of this magnitude are bound to impact a multitude of asset classes, including rates. Treasuries have been particularly volatile, although we have seen 2 -way moves as yields have been caught between haven demand and rising inflation pricing. Our analysis of the current rate s moves is that they have been fairly muted when compared to oil shock s over the past 3 -decades. This is true for both price action and our investor behaviour. Of note has been relatively weak demand for TIPs, a nod to the limited durability of higher oil prices, although this also works against rising nominal yields to the extent that higher prices prevail for an extended period. Additionally, foreign demand remains weak, standing in contra st to prior episodes that saw improving cross border flows. So, while USTs has been generally well behaved given current circumstances, there are signs that higher yields are still possible, particularly if oil prices have yet to plateau. records.text: ECB Preview—Well-Positioned to Respond to the Energy Shock We expect the Governing Council to hold policy rates unchanged on March 19, take stock of the incoming data and focus on the risks posed by the war in Iran. The incoming data (before the onset of the Iran conflict) have been broadly consistent with the December staff projections. The activity indicators have been a bit firmer than expected, including the Q4 GDP composition, the recent business surveys, public spending in Germany and the unemployment rate. At the same time, the wage growth and inflation numbers have been slightly weaker than expected, with compensation per employee 0.2pp below expectations in Q4 and core inflation tracking 0.1pp below the December projections in Q1. But the sharp rise in energy prices since the outbreak of the war poses important risks to the outlook (Exhibit 1). As of March 6—a reasonable guess for the timing of the cutoff point for the technical assumptions—spot oil and prices were up 82% and 48%, respectively. That said, the energy forward curves moved up much less, pointing to expectations for a temporary energy shock. Also, financial conditions have tightened since December with our financial conditions index 18bp tighter between the cutoff points. Our rules of thumb—which are similar to the ECB staff’s—point to materially higher headline inflation, a notable effect on growth but small effects on core inflation. How high this goes will matter for many on the MPC, especially with the Bank looking to anchor inflation expectations after a protracted period of excess price pressures. Moreover, the MPC (and we) will be watching closely how higher energy prices feed through into core inflation. Spillovers into services and non-energy industrial goods prices will be closely monitored. And successive and frequent upside surprises to services CPI could prompt the MPC to pivot firmly away from its easing stance. On the flip side, should pass-through of cost rises be limited, the MPC could be minded to look past the energy shock as a one-off temporary event. Why June over April? Why November? Given the uncertainty in the inflation outlook, we see two preconditions for the next rate cut. One, a resolution to the Iran conflict bringing energy prices down and yields lower. Confidence that energy price moves are indeed temporary, we think, will be crucial for the committee in having any confidence in the inflation outlook. Energy prices and the General Escape Clause The recent surge in energy costs has prompted a debate over fiscal responses at the EU level. At a recent Eurogroup meeting, Italy reportedly requested the activation of the General Escape Clause (GEC), which would temporarily suspend the Stability and Growth Pact's fiscal rules. This request is notable as Italy is among the most exposed of the large euro area economies to the energy shock and possesses limited fiscal room to act unilaterally (for more on this point see recent note). For the GEC to be triggered, a "severe economic downturn" affecting the entire Euro Area is required. Citing this condition, EU Commissioner Dombrovskis stated that activation is not currently possible. The discussion has clearly started, but the likelihood of a coordinated fiscal intervention like the GEC will be a function of future economic developments and energy market volatility. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels – at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. records.text: 13 March 2026 UK Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG What's the case for rate hikes? We don't think the case for rate hikes rests solely on energy prices - despite its potency in shaping inflation expectations. Our view is simple: if Middle East tensions escalate, raising energy prices further and pushing the peak and duration of the energy shock to new levels, we would expect fiscal policy to cushion against the cost of living shock. Indeed, the Government will have many tools at its disposal. A further acceleration in oil prices could see the Government introduce a further extension to the fuel duty freeze. Elevated gas/electricity prices could see the Chancellor push for a targeted and temporary reintroduction of the Energy Price Guarantee. These would cap a lot of the gains in inflation - keeping inflation well below the levels registered in 2022/23. In short, the Government will have measures on hand to curb inflation (and therefore inflation expectations) should it need to. And energy price rises in isolation may not factor into the Bank's calculus – especially if additional fiscal support comes into play. So, what then would put rate hikes on the MPC's mind? The MPC, we think, will want to refrain from fiddling with its policy levers until there is clear evidence that it needs to. The energy shock led to further easing of about 1-1.5pp of GDP. Outright stimulus could complicate the ability of monetary policy to re-anchor inflation to 2%. However, much of the fiscal response was targeted and temporary – they aimed at minimising the rise in energy inflation or defusing its impact. To the extent these targeted measures reduced inflation, they directly assisted what the ECB was trying to achieve with the tightening of monetary policy. It is too soon to know whether fiscal policy will once again try to shield the economy from an energy price shock. The higher prices are and the longer they remain elevated, the more likely a fiscal response becomes. The less targeted the fiscal easing, the greater the risk to inflation persistence and vice versa. In 2022, only 20- 25% of the fiscal measures were targeted. For more, see our note on this. Nonetheless, it is helpful for two reasons: n Firstly, the data is released a month earlier than the data in the first section of the piece. Therefore, it is a helpful predictor of Japanese investors' fixed income activity for the most recent month. This is also borne out in the data; this series predicts net Japanese flows into US Treasuries with 71% R- squared. n Secondly, this data set is helpful as it splits these flows into specific investor groups. We include charts for the investor groups with significant flows: banks (banking accounts), banks (trust accounts), "finance instrument firms" (sell-side firms), life insurance, investment trusts, and "other". The data for February suggests negative net flows into foreign long-term debt, which would mark a reversal of buying trend of USTs in the last couple of years. records.text: Fiscal policy to ease; monetary policy mostly unchanged As noted, most governments in the region attempt to cushion the impact of surging commodity prices on consumers. Exhibit 11 lists a range of price control mechanisms or subsidies already in place. In addition, several countries have already announced ‘ad hoc’ support—for example, South Korea will cap retail fuel prices as of the level at end-February, effective today (March 13), and review these caps every two weeks going forward. This arguably marks the most significant intervention by the Korean government in fuel markets since deregulation nearly three decades ago. Given these actions, fiscal policy is likely to ease in the majority of regional economies as a result of the oil shock. Of course, subsidy spending could be offset by cuts in other areas, but we suspect in most cases the result is likely to be a net loosening. This adds to pre-existing pressures to boost domestic demand: much of the region was already facing a more challenging export environment due to US tariffs and intense competition from Chinese manufacturers. The implications of the energy shock for monetary policy are mixed, with higher inflation and lower growth pointing in different directions. We note that in most regional economies, the starting point for CPI inflation is broadly in line with (DMs) or below (most EMs) central bank targets. We have also raised our estimated risk of recession over the next 12 months by 5pp to 25%, 10pp above the unconditional long-term average but in line with the latest Bloomberg consensus. Implications for the Fed We had previously expected the FOMC to deliver two final 25bp rate cuts in June and September mainly for the purpose of normalizing the funds rate to 3-3.25% once enough progress on inflation had been made. A June start now looks too early under our higher revised inflation forecast, and we are therefore pushing back the two cuts to September and December. By September, we expect both some further labor market softening and progress on underlying inflation to contribute to the case for a cut. Earlier cuts are still possible if the labor market weakens sooner and more substantially than we expect. The weaker February employment report kept concerns about further labor market softening alive, and both lower GDP growth and higher geopolitical risk would make this somewhat more likely. If the labor market softens enough to make a case for cutting earlier, we do not think that concern about the impact of higher oil prices on inflation and inflation expectations would hold the FOMC back. First, a resurgence in growth in spite of geopolitical shocks. This would suggest that the economy is little fazed by the unfolding energy shock and any anticipated weakness in demand as a result of higher energy prices may have been overstated. Put differently, this would signal that the economy may be in a cyclical upswing after a temporary dip, and could risk further lifting the inflation bump. Second, a rapid unwind of the jobless rate. With inflation rising, the MPC will be reticent to see the jobless rate falling. Stronger labour demand would point to an economy heating up as opposed to cooling down - a warning sign for policymakers that there may not be enough slack in the labour market to bring wage growth to target-consistent levels. Indeed, the combination of a jobs market recovery alongside higher inflation (and higher inflation expectations) would raise the risk that wage settlements are ratcheted higher next year – adding to concerns of second-round effects to the policy outlook. Third, another exogenous/endogenous shock.
