records.text: 312/03/2026 Q3: What could be the best opportunities in FX if the market pivots to trading growth more actively? To gauge this, we look at countries where: ▪ inflation is below target, suggesting growth is sluggish and a central bank is unlikely to tighten quickly, and ▪ the trade balance is sensitive to higher energy prices. The lower left quadrant of Figure 1 captures these. The SEK, HUF, ZAR and THB stand out as vulnerable through this lens. As such we would expect these currencies to be most vulnerable in case of a further energy price shock. In contrast, BRL, AUD, MXN and CAD should prove comparatively resilient in this scenario. Q4: How has your view on FX hedging changed since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East? The energy shock has brought about an episode of USD strength in risk-off conditions. This goes against the trend seen since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term, during which the USD has increasingly declined in risk-off. In the case of EURUSD, our modelling suggests that this episode is enough to imply a partial reduction in eurozone investor hedging (see Figure 2). However, it is small, and only enough to offset the rise in the implied FX hedge ratio since the beginning of 2026. Big picture, we think the broader theme of foreign investors being incentivised to raise FX hedge ratios since the beginning of 2025 remains in place. The outlook for inflation remains highly contingent not just on the breadth and duration of the conflict but on the lingering effects of the conflict on the global energy market. Oil at USD80/bbl and gas at EUR50/ MWh would imply moderate and transitory shock, not one that justifies a monetary tightening unless inflation expectations threaten to de-anchor. Growth would be much lower too – a recession would be likely. The ability to trade off weaker growth against higher inflation and ‘look through’ an energy shock would depend on how the ECB perceives the risk of persistent inflation. That is, the risk of a sustained overshoot of the inflation target. records.text: Even in a relatively constructive base case outcome, higher oil prices and uncertainty should lead to weaker GDP growth, higher inflation, and later Fed easing than our economists had previously expected. Exhibit 4 summarizes updated GS baseline forecasts for oil, the US economy, and interest rates, including a 2026 Q4/Q4 real US GDP growth that has been lowered from 2.5% to 2.2%. Our economists continue to expect two 25 bp Fed cuts this year but now expect the next cut will occur in September, rather than June, unless the labor market deteriorates more substantially. Accordingly, the market has recently priced both a deterioration in the outlook for economic growth and a less friendly path of monetary policy. The rotations between cyclical and defensive S&P 500 industries began to signal a weakening economic outlook in early February, even prior to the spike in oil prices. However, that deterioration was accompanied by a decline in short-term interest rates, helping buoy the equity market. As oil has spiked during the past two weeks, however, the continued decline in economic growth pricing has been exacerbated by a steep climb in short-term yields, dragging stocks lower. Today, the market appears to be pricing an outlook for roughly 1.5% GDP growth, below our economists’ forward 4-quarter forecasts but above the lows reached during the growth shocks in April 2025 or August 2024. Assuming we are correct that the muted reaction in FX reflects the insulating effect of front-end rates, and that rates have focused more on the inflation impact of higher oil prices, it therefore follows that a market shift to trading the potential growth impact could drive a more meaningful reaction in FX. Historically, the peak in oil prices during supply shocks does not mark the low in EURUSD. Instead, EURUSD continues depreciating as oil stabilises at elevated levels. One reason for this may be that the market trades the second-order impact of higher oil prices on growth only after oil prices peak. This suggests the market perception changes even with oil prices stable at higher levels (rather than rising). This dynamic is visible through the lens of our BERT framework (see Regime Navigator: Asset and liquid alternatives tilts, dated 4 March). Expanding beyond our baseline scenario, we conduct a stress test across Asia economies for the event of a sustained LNG shortage. Sitting at the top of the risk ladder would be the tech supply-chain economies including Taiwan, Japan, Korea. As such, a severe LNG shortage in Asia could have global repercussions for technology and manufacturing supply chains. Week ahead In the coming week, we turn our focus to the monetary policy meetings in Japan, Australia and Indonesia, along with a flurry of data releases in the region. We expect the BoJ to keep the policy rate unchanged at 0.75% as the geopolitical shocks in Middle East will likely reinforce the Bank’s wait-and-see stance. BI is also expected to stay on hold at 4.75%. Meanwhile, we expect RBA to deliver 25 bps rate hike in an out-of-consensus call, bringing the policy rate to 4.10%, as oil shock introduces a material upside inflation risk. records.text: BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting Preview 13 March 2026 Citi Research 2 Middle East conditions make BoJ policy action more difficult Our base-case scenario has assumed a semiannual rate hike by the BoJ, with the next hike in July. Before tensions escalated in the Middle East, the media reported both hawkish and dovish elements regarding BoJ policy, which in our view suggested a tug of war between the Takaichi administration’s reluctance toward a rate hike and the BoJ’s desire to continue with policy normalization (Figure 1). In this situation we saw the risk as tilted to the hawkish side and pointed to a potential early hike in April depending on the yen exchange rate (Japan Economics: BoJ MPM review: Policy outlook risks lean hawkish). However, the deteriorating Middle East situation has likely made an early move by the BoJ more difficult, and we now see the hawkish risk receding somewhat in the near term. We thought the FX market held the key for a monetary policy decision, but the prospective negative impact of surging oil prices on the Japanese economy probably deprives the BoJ of an early hike option, and some further yen depreciation may well be tolerated. While FX remains an important factor, we expect Middle East conditions to be key at the moment. Figure 1. BoJ-related events/reports in the past month © 2026 Citigroup Inc. Our model suggests that we are unlikely to see material second-round effects in n Euro area core inflation in our baseline scenario where energy prices normalise in coming weeks. But the pass-through could increase materially—with core inflation rising to 3%—if the energy shock continues to build, as captured in a very adverse scenario where disruptions in the flow of energy commodities through the Strait of Hormuz last for two months. Our analysis supports our baseline forecast of unchanged ECB policy, as well as n President Lagarde’s comment that the economy has “greater capacity to absorb shocks” today than in 2022. But our results also highlight that pass-through effects could emerge if the energy crisis intensifies, potentially pushing the ECB into hiking rates. ECB projections: all about sensitivity analysis The forecast update from the ECB should, a priori, come with little news for the base case. A cut-off in mid-February would leave out energy price moves. Data flow until then would trigger marginal changes to the growth and inflation numbers this year, without any meaningful changes to 2027, and none to 2028. Policy would remain in a “good place” compared to that scenario. Of course, there is a possibility that ECB staff work with different cut-off dates given the building energy price shock – Board member Schnabel’s comments earlier this week alluded to this possibility. If technical assumptions were based on last week’s average futures curves and rates and exchange rates, synthetic energy prices (ie the weighted average of gas and oil) would be c 20% higher than the base case this year, 12% next and 5% in 2028. While energy price levels would be higher, the decline over the forecast horizon would be steeper. EURUSD would be 3% lower (adding 10bp to growth and inflation per year using ECB references) and financial conditions arguably tighter. In all, we would expect the ECB to show headline inflation at 2.5-2.6% this year then 1.7-1.8% next. But given the energy price trajectory, we would still assume 2028 inflation to be very close to 2%, not least to remain non-committal on policy implications.

According to IBGE, it accounted for 3.2% of GDP and 15.7% of industrial value added, positioning it as the second‑largest industrial segment, alongside construction (Exhibit 4). A sustained spike in oil prices would mechanically lift revenues in the extractive complex, with a potential upper‑bound contribution of up to 0.2pp to GDP, reflecting both the scale and the export orientation of the sector. However, this positive impulse stands in sharp contrast with the downside risks facing agriculture. Should fertilizer prices rise meaningfully due to disruptions in maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz, the shock would become a net negative for Brazil’s farm sector by 2027. The sensitivity stems from Brazil’s heavy reliance on imported nitrogen‑based fertilizers. The Middle East supplied 22% of Brazil’s nitrogen imports in 2025, and the region accounts globally for 30–40% of urea trade and roughly 45% of sulfur exports – all of which depend on unimpeded transit through the Strait. For the ongoing 2025/26 crop cycle, risk remains limited: most inputs have already been purchased, and major crops – soybeans (harvest underway), first‑crop corn (harvest), second‑crop corn and cotton (planting), and sugarcane (late growth) – have largely completed the fertilization phase. records.text: 13 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 51 Something big in Fed pricing? Today’s chart looks at recent shifts in Fed pricing, as reflected in SOFR futures. There have been two notable drivers over the past six weeks. First, over the month of February, concerns about AI-driven job destruction in coming years – fueled in large part by social media posts – led to a marked re-pricing of Fed cuts in 2027 and 2028. Over this period, prediction market contracts on the US unemployment rate moving above 5.5% this year soared. There was, however, little impact on Fed cuts priced for 2026. Second and more recently, the conflict in Iran and associated oil price shock catalyzed a hawkish Fed re-pricing. These moves have been almost entirely in 2026, reflecting cuts taken out altogether rather than simply pushed out in time. What might lie ahead? While the FOMC would be inclined to look through an energy supply shock, with inflation having run above target for several years, substantial uncertainty about underlying inflation, and ongoing concerns that inflation expectations could un- anchor, the Committee is likely to proceed cautiously with further cuts as long as downside labor market risks seem contained. Morgan Securities plc Global Economic Research 13 March 2026 J P M O R G A N This month’s attacks on Iran point to a sixth global energy supply shock, but the rise in crude oil prices to date does not represent a shock of the magnitude seen in earlier episodes. At $100bbl, Brent crude is less than 35% above its two-year trailing average. To deliver a shock similar in size to the Rus- sian invasion, crude oil prices would need to move close to $150bbl and remain at this elevated level for several months. It will take time for central banks to recognize the magnitude of the shock and assess its lasting impact. But forecasts will immediately bias towards higher inflation and lower growth. Initially, we expect uncertainty to promote caution, against a backdrop of policy stances that are close to neutral in most countries. Consistent with this view, we have pushed back or removed rate cuts for nearly all central banks—except Brazil whose policy stance is highly restrictive. Incoming data are expected to show strong 1Q26 global growth and a March- April CPI inflation bounce but are unlikely to be a catalyst for hikes outside the countries where hikes are already in our forecast (Japan, Australia). records.text: Barclays Research That said, it is difficult to know whether or not there is truly a trade opportunity here. Given that the jet fuel variables only explain c.23% of the variability in CPI airline fares, trying to hedge the category with jet fuel futures could introduce more tracking error than true risk reduction. Moreover, this modeling does not incorporate any demand shift due to either unease regarding the geopolitical situation, or strained household budgets resulting from higher gasoline prices. And the conflict itself remains massively uncertain and is fluctuating widely, so it is far from obvious that the price path assumed above is reasonable. To be sure, a better real-time tracker would be like what Barclays' economists use for the concurrent month, relying on the average transaction value of tickets sold across 16 domestic airlines, including high- and low-cost carriers, sourced from Bloomberg's AL TD database. To that point, rather than emphasize that the scenario laid out above is a likely modal scenario, we hope with this analysis that we gave an example for how the energy price dynamics may bleed into core inflation. The risk that inflation expectations are ratcheted higher is no longer benign, bringing back the prospect of second-round effects, including rising wage settlements. In short, timing of any further easing is more uncertain than before. Second, this is not 2022. The economy is in a very different place than it was four years ago. Fiscal policy is tightening sizeably. Monetary policy is restrictive. GDP growth is weakening. Inflation expectations are slowing (for now). And the labour market has seen a sizeable loosening, with the unemployment rate up 1pp over the last year. We wouldn't be surprised if the MPC even pushes back on recent market moves in the front-end, emphasizing the Bank's framework that despite its primary focus on price stability, "there will be occasions when inflation will depart from the target as a result of shocks and disturbances" – similar to what the MPC noted in 2022. Third, the MPC may need to approach further rate cuts with caution. The once assumed disinflation path to 2% looks unlikely given expected pump price moves. The rise in energy prices will also lift inflation expectations. And the Bank of England would face another year with CPI tracking well above target. Downside risks to inflation, we think, will no longer remain base case for some of the swing votes on the MPC. This may require policy to stand still for a little while longer until the dust settles

records.text: 13 March 2026 Focus Europe Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG The vulnerability of inflation expectations In a recent speech, ECB Executive Board Member Isabel Schnabel provided a stark assessment of the current state of inflation expectations in the euro area, highlighting their increased fragility in the post-pandemic environment. According to Schnabel, the prolonged period of high inflation has left expectations more vulnerable to shocks than they were in the past. She pointed to data from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES), which reveals that despite the significant progress made on disinflation, median expectations remain elevated across horizons. More concerning, mean inflation expectations had already started "creeping up", even before the recent energy price shock stemming from geopolitical tensions in Iran (indicating the distribution is becoming more skewed). This suggests a latent instability, where the public's view of future inflation is less firmly anchored to the central bank's target. Schnabel's remarks underscore the heightened risks facing policy makers today. She argues that in this environment, the "costs of misjudging the balance between supply and demand are higher". The fragility of expectations means that any new inflationary impulse, such as an energy shock from the latest Iran conflict, could more easily dislodge public confidence and reignite price pressures. This contrasts with the pre-pandemic era, where expectations were more robustly anchored. So

records.text: 11 March 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG onwards, even if the structural difficulties of reunification also began to weigh on the economy despite the large fiscal expansion accompanying it (Figure 1). Perhaps the silver lining to the historical analogy is that the Gulf War and, thus, the spike in oil prices, proved to be relatively short-lived. Yet, the episode also shows that even a transient oil price shock can have persistent effects on the economy, especially if it leads to a tightening in financial conditions. While the Bundesbank perhaps reacted excessively to the oil price shock of 1990, financial markets will continue to price at least some risk of ECB rate hikes as long as the Iran war reverberates in energy markets. So, even if the duration of the current Iran war should be measured in weeks rather than months, the surge in energy prices will weigh on Germany's trade balance, dampen consumer spending, and exacerbate existing competitiveness challenges for German industry. More broadly, the Iran war has reignited uncertainty and tightened financial conditions just as global trade tensions appeared to be receding (Figure 2). While this would increase the risk of pass-through into core inflation, ultimately it would also be a drag on labor markets and inflation in the medium term. We believe rates markets are getting complacent. Global bonds sold off further over the week as even as oil prices peaked intra-week at nearly $120, uncertainty as measured by oil implied volatility has continued to rise ( Figure 1). The front end of the gilt market again led the global market sell-off with yields about 30bp higher than a week ago, followed by Bunds and US at about 15-20bp ( Figure 2). The sell-off is being led by inflation breakevens, particularly in the UK and euro area ( Figure 3). Expectations of hikes before year-end by the ECB (+43bp) and BoE (+22bp) are getting entrenched even as the Fed is expected to still cut, though just 20bp. We believe this divergence reflects the facts that the inflation shock is perceived to be larger in the euro area and the UK, and the Fed has a dual mandate instead of just inflation ( Figure 4). Rates markets seem too squarely focused on the inflation shock and not so much on the adverse growth shock, should elevated oil levels persist, which now seems to be getting reflected in other asset classes. In addition to the oil shock, Asia is exposed to heightened LNG shortage risks due to its heavy reliance on LNG imports, thin inventories, and vulnerability to supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. On the data front, China’s CPI inflation rose to a three year high, while Jan–Feb trade flows surged above expectations. In India, takeaways from recent macro tours suggest that the policy response is likely to be back loaded, with near term efforts focused on supply augmentation—particularly for LNG and LPG. In Japan, rising oil prices threaten the outlook for positive real wage growth, potentially weighing on household consumption. In Indonesia, the fiscal deficit widened in Feb, with pressures building amid higher oil prices. Uncertainty around the inflation outlook has risen amid tensions involving Iran, given that over one third of China’s oil imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, we expect the MPC next week to sound cautious but signal optionality to resume cuts later. The steepening in the broader front-end, like SONIA M6/M7 (NB: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss), looks at odds with growth risk from energy and jobs risk from AI. However, we refrain from fresh dovish trades following a painful week. BoE pricing has been on quite a journey. Figure 5 shows the pricing of cumulative MPC dates for 2026 for every day since the conflict began. The starting point was over 50bp of cuts priced, 20bp of which was for next week’s meeting. As of close 12 March, there is now a cumulative 20bp of hikes priced as worries grow over a lasting shock to energy supply. The average (absolute) daily reassessment of end- 2026 pricing has been 13bp. There are already some signs that the GBP front-end is overreacting. For example, following hawkish ECB speak on Wednesday (see earlier section), MPC pricing added more hike premium than ECB pricing. The comments that hikes could come sooner were made by the ECB’s Kazimir (see Bloomberg 11Mar26) whose starting point was pre-existing dissatisfaction with the disinflationary progress. We do not expect a verdict on the medium-term outlook next week. We have devised three broad, illustrative scenarios as helpful guides to possible ECB policy choices, and summarize them in this note. Macroeconomic projections | Inflation up in 2026 and down in 2027 in the baseline: We assume the cutoff of the assumptions underlying the March projections was pushed to 3 March instead of 25 Feb. This will allow the baseline to incorporate some impact of the recent energy prices surge, albeit in a smoothed manner, since oil and natural gas prices will reflect an average of futures observed over the 10 days preceding the cutoff. With that, we expect the baseline projections to show inflation above target in 2026 (2.2%Y) and then below in 2027 (1.7%Y). Growth is likely to be revised only a touch downward (-10bp in 2026 and 2027). Alternative scenario showing a recession? The projections will also likely come with alternative scenarios. We flag the Dec-23 ECB scenario of a "partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz" showing a -70bp hit to growth, on the back of higher energy prices, uncertainty and lower global demand. records.text: M Idea 2 Canada Economics: What the oil disruption could mean for the Bank of Canada Arunima Sinha and Mayank Phadke Bank of Canada Implications: Lower bar for hikes, risks of a hike at the July meeting. Our baseline view is that the Bank of Canada (BoC) will remain on hold through the rest of this year, with the first rate hike occurring in 1Q27. This reflects the current macro starting point of excess supply and a softer cyclical backdrop in the Canadian economy. While the ToTEM framework mechanically points toward a policy tightening following an oil price shock, we are cautious about interpreting this signal directly. The model’s results should be understood as deviations from steady state rather than from current conditions. Although higher oil prices support domestic demand through income and wealth channels, they do not materially feed through to core inflation. Moreover, a larger or more persistent commodity shock could dampen U.S. and global growth, creating negative spillovers to Canadian non-commodity exports that offset some of the domestic gains. At the same time, the risks to our baseline skew toward earlier tightening, potentially as early as July 2026 if the oil shock proves persistent. Recent BoC communications suggest that the bar for a hike may be somewhat lower. records.text: M Idea 2 Core PCE inflation came in strong in 1Q, but deceleration is coming Our view that core PCE inflation would accelerate in 1Q26 was confirmed this week following February’s CPI print on Wednesday and today’s release of January PCE prices. January core PCE came in below expectations but still firm at 0.36% m/m (vs. 0.50% MS and 0.4% consensus), with strength across both services and goods. The downside surprise appears largely methodological: The key driver was legal services in PCE. Instead of the usual approach of inferring legal services from CPI (which would have implied roughly ~11% m/m in that category), the BEA appears to have leaned on PPI legal services instead (1.8% m/m). That choice likely shaved close to 10bp off core PCE. The main uncertainty is whether this methodological change persists in coming months. Following the CPI print, we are now tracking February core PCE at 0.42%, pointing to another firm reading. If our forecasts are correct, these two prints would push the 3 month and 6 month annualized pace of core PCE to 4.67% and 3.54% in February, respectively—elevated sequential inflation rates. That said, we believe the acceleration is temporary and that core inflation should begin to decelerate from 2Q onward, opening the door for the Fed to cut rates. Why? For three main reasons. Also, it will be hard for Lagarde to affirm they are still in a good place. How she phrases that could be taken as a signal of imminent policy action. Our conviction in rate cuts to below 2% in 2027, driven by an inflation undershoot, remains unbroken, however. The risk balance around our current base case of cuts in Mar/Jun-27 has moved from earlier to tentatively later cuts to below 2%. But even if the ECB hikes in the summer, by a max 50-75bp, our conviction that the policy rate will be no higher than current levels by end-27 – and more likely below 2% – is intact. If they hike, can they go in April? records.text: Bank regulation and capital requirements In prepared remarks at the Cato Institute Policy Forum, Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman outlined the framework for Basel III and bank capital rules. The proposal would modernize the framework and align it closely with the global Basel III standard. We expect the proposal to be released in coming weeks. In her remarks: We expect the Basel III proposal to result in a small increase in requirements for the largest banks, similar to what is expected in the UK. The G-SIB surcharge proposal would result in a modest decrease in the surcharges, which addresses the recent increases in this requirement that deviated from risk. Together, these proposals would decrease the requirements by a small amount. • Basel III: Banks would move to calculating risk-based requirements using a single approach• rather than maintaining two capital ratios currently (standardized and advanced approach). Some things worth noting are the changes to the market risk calculations to improve the methodology to better capture losses in stressed conditions that also take into account illiquid positions. Standardized calculations would be applied across banks, less so for simpler banks and internal models would be allowed where appropriate. records.text: Given the speed and scale of the moves, the key question has been if the pricing of the ECB's policy path is reasonable and if one should follow or fade the sell-off in ERZ6. As we highlighted last week, we are not comfortable in fading this repricing and find it in the conceivable realm of what can be realised should the energy price shock broaden or even just persist. How well growth holds up in this energy repricing shock, whether fiscal support is offered to affected consumers and industries, and how targeted or widespread this support is, are all crucial variables to determine how fast and how far the ECB has to go should they feel the need to adjust policy. As things stand, market pricing suggests insurance rate hikes from the ECB rather than a protracted rate hike cycle. After all, beyond Z6, the market only prices c.5bp of hikes for 2027 and another 8bp of hikes for 2028. In this light, we had initiated a z6z7 steepener at 11.5bp last week. Our premise was that should the increase in energy prices persist, the market should price a more protracted cycle and hence the slope between z6z7 can increase. records.text: Expecting Stronger Price Control Measures; Core CPI Inflation Revised Up Slightly The higher energy prices forecast has led us to revise up our core CPI (excludes fresh food) inflation forecasts, mainly for 2026 (average core CPI to 2.0% yoy, a 0.1 pp upward revision from our early March forecast, and 0.4 pp from our pre-war forecast). Our inflation forecasts incorporate price control measures for various fuels, such as gasoline and diesel oil, recently announced by Prime Minister Takaichi1. We also assume the resumption of price control measures for electricity and gas charges in summer and winter 2026 as well. Accordingly, the revisions to our inflation forecasts are small relative to the magnitude of the upward revision to our commodity price forecasts. We also ran a stress test on our inflation forecasts based on the adverse scenarios on commodity prices described earlier in this note. Under the adverse scenario with a relatively small impact, the upside to the inflation rate would be modest. However, under a severely adverse scenario in which Brent crude oil prices temporarily reach US$150/bbl, we expect average core CPI inflation in 2026 to reach 2.4%, peaking at 3.3% yoy. The peak inflation rate is lower than in the stress test we published last week (which showed peak core CPI inflation of 3.5% assuming crude prices temporarily reach US$100/bbl), because we now assume implementation of larger price control measures for electricity, gas, and gasoline. Note: Green represents rate cut scenarios and red represents rate hike scenarios How likely do these conditions appear at present? We continue to think they’re unlikely. The labor market remains in a long-prevailing state of low-hiring and low-firing. Our recent work demonstrated that the decline in the hiring rate since 2019 is equally explained by cyclical conditions (i.e., sensitivity to monetary policy) and weak labor supply (i.e., immigration policy) (see “Disentangling the forces behind weak hiring”). Thus, even if constrained labor supply is leading to tighter conditions in immigration-sensitive sectors (see construction), the ongoing oil price shock should dampen demand and hiring intentions, preventing the labor market from reaccelerating. Indeed, FRB/US simulations show that oil price shocks tend to lead to higher unemployment (see “Impact of oil price shocks a ‘frack’-tion of what they once were”). Consequently, we see the more likely path towards rate hikes as operating through accelerating wages and prices alongside a noticeable rise in inflation expectations that forces the Fed’s hand. Energy prices and the General Escape Clause The recent surge in energy costs has prompted a debate over fiscal responses at the EU level. At a recent Eurogroup meeting, Italy reportedly requested the activation of the General Escape Clause (GEC), which would temporarily suspend the Stability and Growth Pact's fiscal rules. This request is notable as Italy is among the most exposed of the large euro area economies to the energy shock and possesses limited fiscal room to act unilaterally (for more on this point see recent note). For the GEC to be triggered, a "severe economic downturn" affecting the entire Euro Area is required. Citing this condition, EU Commissioner Dombrovskis stated that activation is not currently possible. The discussion has clearly started, but the likelihood of a coordinated fiscal intervention like the GEC will be a function of future economic developments and energy market volatility. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Third, the February CPI print confirmed continued deceleration in the underlying trend in shelter inflation. We think it is increasingly clear that rent inflation will soften over the rest of 2026. The key question is whether monthly readings fall below the pre COVID trend of 0.26% m/m. After this week’s CPI release, we took some signal and revised down our shelter inflation path to a pace slightly below the pre COVID average, at around 0.24% m/m. Taken together, these three factors point to a near term deceleration in core PCE inflation. Are there risks to this outlook from the recent upswing in oil prices? The main risk would be a potential de anchoring of inflation expectations, but we assign a low probability to that scenario. As we have shown in recent work, if inflation expectations remain well behaved, the effect of oil shocks on core inflation is limited. The FRB/US model implies a near zero impact on core inflation, and our own dynamic estimates suggest roughly 3bp for every 10% increase in oil prices—but only if the oil shock is persistent enough to generate second round effects. For the Fed, we see risks skewed toward later—and potentially more—cuts than in our current forecast (two cuts in June and September this year). Given heightened uncertainty, the Fed may choose to wait for clearer evidence of deceleration in core inflation. records.text: Iran conflict curtails energy supply US/Israeli strikes on Iran over the past two weeks, and Iranian responses (including attacks on neighboring countries), have led to a sharp reduction in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the shutdown of significant energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf region. Although the available data suggests the frequency of Iranian missile and drone strikes has fallen by 80-90% since the early days of the conflict, reports of damage to ships and infrastructure continue, and vessel traffic through the Strait remains minimal. As a result, our commodities research team has changed their base-case assumption to reflect a longer period of disruption, and now assumes a longer three-week period of very low Strait of Hormuz flows before a gradual one-month recovery (Exhibit 1 is reproduced from their comment). They also assume a larger policy response from global strategic oil reserve releases that nearly halves the hit to commercial oil inventories in the short term. The net result is an average Brent crude oil price of over $100/bbl in March, falling to $85/bbl in April, and then drifting down to the low $70s/bbl later in the year. Should the disruption to oil flows prove longer-lived, oil prices could reach higher peaks and end the year at higher levels. The recent MXN sell-off trimmed long positions, reducing the need to roll those exposures by selling FX points and thereby relieving the notable downside pressure on the basis seen in recent months. Stronger USD inflow meets tax season: We believe the MXN cross-currency basis could experience a seasonal upside push in March-April due to higher USD inflows from remittances and increased MXN cash demand linked to the tax season. Since 2010, the 1-year MXN basis has tended to rise on average by about 17bp over February-April (excluding 2020 and 2018 due to data quality issues), as shown in Figure 1. Historically, March often sees a rise in remittance inflows. This is largely because American economic activity picks up as the weather warms (e.g. more construction projects), boosting disposable income for Mexican workers in the US (Figure 2). The seasonal surge in USD inflows via remittances lessens local USD funding pressure and could push the near-end basis higher. As a result, in a higher inflation environment driven by a negative supply shock, bonds tend not to provide a good hedge for equities. Consequently, bonds should carry a higher risk premium. This is indeed what was observed following the oil shock of the late 1970s. Finally, any additional government support to cushion the impact of higher oil prices should also support higher term premia. Thus, the positioning- driven decline in long-end term premia in Europe was, if anything, contrary to what the macro impact of higher oil prices should have implied. In HICPx, the 1y1y forward has clearly outperformed its usual beta to energy and nominal rates, with current market pricing c.15bp above model-implied levels ( Figure 1). In line with our expectations, 1y1y HICPx has likely benefited from a positive risk premium increasingly priced in the 1y+ part of the HICPx curve, reflective of second-round inflation effects from higher energy prices eventually boosting EA core inflation and inflation expectations. Further out, performance in intermediate forwards has been broadly consistent with their respective betas, with both 2y3y and 5y5y HICPx ( Figure 2 & Figure 3) close to model-implied levels. In the back- end, 10y10y HICPx has recently underperformed ( Figure 4), standing c.4bp cheap relative to the model-implied levels, potentially offering good entry levels for structurally long inflation views / cheap medium-term inflation risk hedges. records.text: arch analyst account. Key Takeaways As geopolitical tension in the Middle East escalated, the JGB curve initially bear- steepened as popular flattener trades were unwound. Markets believe prolonged geopolitical escalation would make it difficult for the BoJ to hike in the very near term, while pricing higher term premium on the longer end given the risk of the BoJ falling behind the curve. That said, if tensions last longer than markets anticipate, we see a risk that growth concerns > inflation concerns at some point. In that event, we would see the JGB curve shifting from bear-steepening to twist- steepening, with long-end JGBs likely facing selling pressure from pension funds’ rebalancing. As such, we maintain the JGB 5s30s steepener. We also maintain receive April MPM OIS, as the BoJ would likely take time to assess the impact of higher energy prices on underlying inflation. Yesterday, the 2-year Treasury yield jumped about 10bps to 3.75%, its highest level since late August and roughly 20bps above the effective fed funds rate. The recent repricing has reflected a significant re-think of the Fed outlook this year in response to recent events in the Middle East, with the market moving from ~60bps of cuts priced two weeks ago to ~20bps at present. Most strikingly, the market has moved to price a roughly 25% probability of a rate hike this year. With global central banks shifting in a hawkish direction, a question that was almost unthinkable two weeks ago is now being more heavily debated: Could the Fed raise rates in 2026? From a fundamental perspective, we think there are two preconditions for a rate hike this year. (Note that the following only applies to hike conditions for 2026; there are scenarios where the Fed could hike at later dates simply because inflation stays at elevated levels and does not show signs of returning to target.) First, downside risks to the labor market need to be eliminated. The past two years have shown that the Fed is responsive to weak labor market conditions and downside risks even in the face of elevated inflation. Hikes likely require something more, though. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 13 March 2026 15 Emerging EMEA Jean-Michel Saliba MLI (UK) What are the possible durations and outcomes of the war? The situation remains fluid. Official pronouncements as well as speakers from the series of conference calls we conducted suggested a base case of about four weeks for an effective US/Israeli campaign. However, there is much uncertainty on the timeline. Iran pronouncements suggest a likely strategy to make the conflict costly and lengthy to change the US calculus. Escalated global costs could shorten the duration of the conflict; a wider set of conflict goals could extend it. Experts suggested the most likely end for the conflict could be through a decision by US President Trump. Low trust among belligerents makes a negotiated ceasefire more complicated to achieve. US President Trump articulated a number of goals, including on the nuclear front (with the stock of highly enriched uranium still at large), military front (degrading ballistic missile capabilities, in particular) and regime leadership. Experts in our calls viewed the regime as likely to survive, although perhaps altered. Experts concurred that the Venezuela model is hard to transpose into Iran and suggested that regime change is a challenging political goal. The major risk to markets, beyond shipping, remains the possibility of permanent losses of energy production in the Gulf. As we learned in the aftermath of “Liberation Day”, at some point, the selloff in oil prices or financial assets (stocks and/or bonds) start signaling an economic cost of the war that is hard to ignore and may induce de- escalation and exploring creative ways to end the war, even if the original objectives of the war have not been achieved. This feedback effect is particularly important in an electoral year, and it becomes more important as we approach the midterm elections since gasoline prices become an easily observable signal of the war. This is one possible interpretation of the price action observed this week. Tail risk scenarios should be less likely If we apply this framework to the different scenarios, a quick resolution of the war would have a very limited impact on the global economy. In turn, a more protracted but moderate regime hardlining scenario would need to be monitored as the shocks would have a very heterogenous impact on different economies, but they would be manageable with timely fiscal and monetary policy.

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 13 March 2026 3 Tail risks scenarios where the war extends into the 3rd and 4th quarters represent a sizable stagflationary shock for the global economy, risking a global recession. But this is precisely one reason why those scenarios have much lower probability of occurrence, as the expected economic costs would align incentives for de-escalation. A shock with heterogenous growth effects Of course, initial conditions matter, and an energy shock would have a more aggressive impact on Europe and Asia, which are for the most part energy importers, as opposed to the US which is now less energy dependent than before. But in the US case, given the recent run-up in asset prices, a tightening of global financial conditions could trigger contagion into other markets like private credit, exacerbating the initial shock. The AI- related investment boom in the US could be impaired as the sector is energy-intensive. A story of chokepoints Last but not least, the outcome of the war will shape the dynamics of the race to influence chokepoints: the US has incentives to increase control of strategic energy supply and advanced chip technology, to counteract China’s dominance in critical minerals and rare earths. Developments from now until the Trump-Xi meeting in April will be key to watch beyond the very fluid dynamics of the US-Iran conflict.

This has undermined the previously-anticipated disinflation path, raising concerns about higher inflation, lower GDP, and increased unemployment. As a result, we think the MPC will adopt a dovish "wait-and-see" approach on March 19th. We anticipate a less divided vote than in February, with seven members likely to vote to keep the Bank Rate unchanged, while two members (Dhingra and Taylor) opt for a quarter-point rate cut. This shift, we think, will be driven by the change in perception of downside risks to inflation and a change in risk management considerations due to the energy price shock. While we still expect two rate cuts this year, recent events have pushed back our previous expectations. We now anticipate the next rate cut in Q2-26 (June), contingent on more evidence of falling core inflation and a potential resolution of the Iran conflict, followed by one more cut in Q4-26. The bar to reach a neutral stance has effectively been raised, requiring additional evidence of muted second- round effects and a sustained downtrend in wage settlements. By compiling those, we are able to estimate that Eurosystem forecasters see a 10% persistent shock on oil prices as lifting EA inflation by 23bp in the first year and 12bp in the second, with a 10% hit on natural gas prices increasing HICP by 13bp in the first year and 15bp the second. records.text: UK Watch | 12 March 2026 5 FX: Backseat burner The current geopolitical backdrop has taken the steam out of the macro trade as investors continue to be guided by developments in the oil price. This suggests that the March meeting will likely be a non-event with the BoE operating in a void of relevant information on the impact on the economy. With UK rates having followed G10 counterparts in pricing out rate cuts/pricing in rate hikes, a no change in rates seems to be the least controversial outcome for this meeting. Echoes of 2022 will however loom large for the BoE who will have some back data on how the situation could evolve. A wait-and-see approach seems prudent for now and at a minimum, near-term rate cuts are likely to be off the table. The crucial element is whether the government will announce measures to stave off further cost of living pressures on households and thus ring fence the need for rate hikes. That remains to be seen in a period of higher than usual uncertainty. For now, we expect GBP to follow the broader trend in FX which has seen the pound more resilient than may have been anticipated on a lower terms of trade hit. That resilience will be tested in the coming weeks as we approach the May local elections and focus returns to domestic politics. Our sense is that this may put the brakes on further GBP upside though it is not clear whether there will be appetite for a change in leadership against the current backdrop. records.text: licy space as we approach neutral. For now, our base case is that this energy shock is not as significant as the 2022 one, but the monetary policy response will be—rightfully—cautious. As things stand, the structural consequences of this shock differ significantly from the 2022 shock. Not only is the economy at a different point in the economic cycle (more on this below), but the adjustment to imports is fundamentally less disruptive. Whereas in 2022, the loss of Russian gas could be considered a loss of gas “stock, ” i.e., a permanent absence of a supply source, the shock today is so far predominantly a flow issue where a marginal supply issue has triggered a (smaller) increase in global energy prices. From the UK’s perspective, the energy supply risk now comes from the marginal US supply being diverted away from Europe, rather than the loss of Middle Eastern natural gas directly. records.text: Monitoring Pass-through ECB officials will therefore closely monitor the size and likely persistence of the energy shock. In addition, we expect policymakers to focus on the following early indicators of second-round effects. First, officials will watch for any changes in inflation expectations (Exhibit 8, left). The ECB monitors a range of measures, including its own survey of professional forecasters (SPF), consumers (CES), and firms (SAFE). Some national central banks (for example, Banque de France and Banca d’Italia) also run their own survey and forecast aggregators (such as Consensus Economics) provide alternative estimates. Moreover, changes in the distribution of expectations can signal shifts in the central tendency. Inflation expectations are currently narrowly centred around the 2% target, but policymakers would likely pay close attention to the emergence of a “right tail” like in 2022 (Exhibit 8, right). Second, policymakers will monitor the frequency of price resets. The ECB collects micro data on the direction, size, and frequency of price changes, which can help inform in real time how a shock is transmitting to prices. For instance, a pick-up in the size and frequency of price increases usually implies that faster and stronger inflation dynamics are underway (Exhibit 9, left). This information, however, is not readily available to market participants. As an alternative to monitor pricing dynamics, we have used price surveys—such as the PMIs and from the Europe

records.text: M Idea 4 Macroeconomic Projections: Alternative Scenarios – Looking Past the Baseline European Economics Team A Baseline and (likely) a couple of alternative scenarios March Projections | What to do? As per usual in March, the ECB will publish updated projections prepared by ECB staff. What could have been a relatively smooth round until the end of February became a much more complicated exercise just before its finalization. We think the baseline will reflect relatively soft assumptions for oil and gas prices (and hence inflation and growth) and will likely be accompanied by one or more alternative scenarios that could be significantly more severe. For those, we looked back at the ECB's analysis of the impact of tensions in the Strait of Hormuz within the Dec-23 projection, as well as the series of boxes on the energy crisis the ECB published throughout 2022. Recapping Dec-25 alternative scenarios: Before digging into more detail, it seems useful to recall what we know about ECB macro elasticities to oil and natural gas price shocks. Exhibit 2 shows the most adverse path envisaged in the alternative scenarios from the Dec-25 round: with oil prices up to ~77.5$/bbl (vs 64$/bbl in the baseline) and natural gas prices peaking at ~35€/MWh (vs ~30€/MWh in the baseline), headline inflation was projected ca 50bp above baseline in 2026-27, while the hit to growth was limited, ca -10bp each year. records.text: European Rates Weekly 12 March 2026 Citi Research 4 watchful and reassess the risk-reward should hike premium to end-2026 comfortably exceed 50bp on any oversized reaction to the ECB meeting. Bearish risk rising for the long-end from fiscal, with Bunds tracking UST. We noted above that 10yr Bunds are only 10bp higher since the last ECB meeting on 5 February, but the increase is closer to 30bp since the conflict began – Figure 4. Last week, we suggested a bearish correction was arguably due and that we weren’t inclined to fade the sell-off. Instead, our base case was for 10yr Bund yields to maintain broader range-trading by settling around 2.75-3%. That is still base case, but bearish risks are rising as the market begins to focus on the fiscal consequences of the conflict. On this, we don’t just mean the possibility of energy support help in Europe but also defence spending in the US with Bunds still tracking USTs closely. This could also help re-steepen European back-ends following the washout flattening in 10s30s. A quick final thought on the potential early departure of President Lagarde: Prior to the conflict, we thought the most interesting item for this meeting might be whether President Lagarde informed her colleagues of her intention to stand down early. Events have taken over, and talk of succession has quietened, but it is still something to look out for at the coming ECB meetings. For our thoughts, see European Rates Weekly: What’s the rush?. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 operation, separate from the monetary policy stance, we discuss our outlook for the program here. FOMC participants have made few, if any, remarks about how purchases are likely to evolve. Our outlook calls for bill purchases of $40bn per month through mid-May and then $7bn per month thereafter. If so, the Fed could make an announcement at its April 29 FOMC meeting about a downshift in the pace of bill purchases. The statement: Still an easing bias, and some backsliding on a stabilizing labor market We look for minimal changes to the FOMC statement. We think the Fed will revert back to its previous description of the unemployment rate having "edged up but remains low" rather than "shown some signs of stabilization." We say this in light of the February employment report which revealed 92,000 fewer jobs and 69,000 in downward revisions to the prior two months of employment. Importantly, we expect the statement to retain its forward bias through "the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate." As we discuss below, we think the committee will be prepared to look through any rise in headline inflation from higher oil prices as opposed to reducing or eliminating guidance about further policy normalization. Elsewhere, we think the description of inflation as "remaining somewhat elevated" will remain, though there is some chance the statement makes a reference to oil prices having moved higher since th

M Idea 6 More progress on bank capital reform On Thursday, Fed Vice-Chair for Supervision Bowman previewed upcoming changes to Basel III endgame and the G-SIB surcharge. We see four main takeaways: 1. The proposal updated the parameters — or coefficients — that determine the impact of firm's activities on the G-SIB surcharge. This better reflects recent changes in the financial system. 2. The proposal revises the surcharge component that accounts for risk associated with short-term funding, which was originally intended to represent 20% of the surcharge. Instead it represents roughly 30%. 3. The proposal reduces incentives to make year-end adjustments to balance sheets by requiring G-SIBs to calculate certain systemic risk indicators as an average of their daily or monthly values, rather than the year-end value. 4. To reduce cliff effects and increase sensitivity to changes in a firm's risk profile, the proposal assigns surcharges in increments of 10bp rather than 50bp. Changes 1, 3, and 4 were in-line with our bank analyst's expectations (see Your Guide to the Coming Endgame), while we believe 2 will be incrementally supportive for increasing dealer financing intermediation capacity and bullish for swap spreads. Some of our own recent research has examined the stability of several inflation expectations measures for the euro area. The results of our framework suggest that while there was no immediate threat of inflation expectations de-anchoring (absent a large shock), households inflation expectations showed a higher level of ambiguity and fragility compared to inflation expectations of professionals and financial markets, putting them at the greatest risk of de-anchoring. Furthermore, the broad consensus in the academic literature is that both energy and food prices have a high salience in the formation of household inflation expectations, making households especially vulnerable to the current situation.1 President Lagarde has often stated that while policy is currently in "a good place" it is not a fixed place. The ECB could react to the Iran conflict if they believe medium- term price stability is threatened, and one of the channels through which this threat could manifest is inflation expectations. records.text: Iran conflict curtails energy supply US/Israeli strikes on Iran over the past two weeks, and Iranian responses (including attacks on neighboring countries), have led to a sharp reduction in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the shutdown of significant energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf region. Although the available data suggests the frequency of Iranian missile and drone strikes has fallen by 80-90% since the early days of the conflict, reports of damage to ships and infrastructure continue, and vessel traffic through the Strait remains minimal. As a result, our commodities research team has changed their base-case assumption to reflect a longer period of disruption, and now assumes a longer three-week period of very low Strait of Hormuz flows before a gradual one-month recovery (Exhibit 1 is reproduced from their comment). They also assume a larger policy response from global strategic oil reserve releases that nearly halves the hit to commercial oil inventories in the short term. The net result is an average Brent crude oil price of over $100/bbl in March, falling to $85/bbl in April, and then drifting down to the low $70s/bbl later in the year. Should the disruption to oil flows prove longer-lived, oil prices could reach higher peaks and end the year at higher levels. After President’s Trump’s “the war is very complete, pretty much” statement on Monday evening the G10 total has subsequently dropped to 220bp but, remains significantly above pre-conflict levels. There is no nuance here; for the market it’s all about inflation.. Policy simulations with our approximation of the ECB’s macro model point to unchanged rates, unless strong second-round effects emerge (Exhibit 8). We find that ECB policy remains on hold under our baseline forecast under either a Taylor rule or an optimal control policy given the lack of second-round effects in core inflation. Interestingly, the policy paths under the Taylor rule and optimal control look quite different in our very adverse scenario. The former implies two hikes (as the Taylor rule responds to the spike in core inflation) while the latter leans against the weakness in growth by cutting rates. These simulations emphasise the uncertainty around the policy outlook, stemming both how the economy evolves and the ECB’s reaction function (given the trade-off between growth and inflation). This analysis supports our forecast of unchanged policy rates unless the economy is pushed into the very adverse scenario (Exhibit 9). The divided nature of the MPC means that individual members will have differing views over the likely impact on inflation, but it will boil down to distinguishing between temporary energy-driven inflation that it might have the luxury of looking though versus more persistent underlying price pressures that cannot be ignored. While headline inflation remained steady in February for the third consecutive month, foreign-produced inflation stayed firmly negative at -1.6% y/y, down from -1.5% in Jan, in sharp contrast with domestic inflation at 0.6% y/y (slightly on the rise from 0.5% in Jan). This divergence underscores the persistent deflationary drag from the strong franc. To note, February was also a key month for rent indexation, an important indicator for the SNB’s monetary-policy pass-through given the link between rents and mortgage rates. Rent inflation eased further to 1.4% y/y, down from 1.6% in Q4, suggesting that the pass-through of the easing monetary stance is ongoing but showing signs of deceleration. It is worth flagging that our preferred measure of domestic bottom-up seasonally adjusted inflation (available up to January) remains comfortably within the SNB’s 0-2% target range, but has also slowed to 0.6% y/y, down from 1.1% in December. This reinforces the view that Swiss price dynamics are likely to remain subdued for now. records.text: The Impact of Higher Oil Prices on Our Economic Forecasts Based on our new oil forecasts, our rules of thumb, these historical lessons, and the details of the February CPI report, we have raised our December 2026 headline PCE inflation forecast by 0.8pp to 2.9% and our core PCE forecast by 0.2pp to 2.4%. In our strategists’ upside oil price scenario, we see headline PCE inflation at 3.3% (with a peak of 4½% in the spring) and core inflation at 2.5% in December 2026. Under their severe upside scenario, headline PCE would be 4.0% (with a peak of 5% in the spring) and core PCE would be 2.7%. We have also lowered our 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth forecast by 0.3pp to 2.2% (or 2.6% on a full-year basis), as shown in Exhibit 9. This reflects a drag from higher oil prices, tighter financial conditions, and higher geopolitical risk that is partially offset by an increase in defense orders. The pickup in defense output will be constrained because production of much of the weaponry that is being most rapidly depleted is already at maximum capacity. GDP growth would be 2.1% Q4/Q4 or 2.5% on a full-year basis in our upside risk scenario for oil prices and it would be 1.9% Q4/Q4 or 2.4% on a full-year basis in our more extreme upside scenario shown. In 2026, the debt ratio is projected to be broadly the same as in 2022 for the "big four" and generally for all Euro Area Member States, with the only difference being Greece (Figure 9). "i-g" gap. While the stock of debt is broadly similar, the elements affecting debt dynamics are to some extent different. Starting from the classical debt accumulation equation, the change in the debt ratio (Δd_t) = ((i-g)/(1+g))d_(t-1) - pb_t. with "i" equal to the average cost of the debt, "g" the nominal GDP growth, "d" the debt ratio and "pb" the primary balance. If (i-g) is positive, the debt ratio increases, all else being equal. Back in 2022, the (i-g) gap was negative for all Member States, naturally reducing debt. The economy was re-emerging from the COVID shock. Tourism was a key factor supporting growth. On top of that, NGEU was providing additional support to peripheral countries, while interest rates were low as the ECB had just started its tightening cycle in mid-2022 (Figure 10). Right now, we are in a different situation. The (i-g) gap is set to become less supportive for debt dynamics (a positive gap or neutral at best, for more see our recent note on fiscal developments here ). Although the economy has proven resilient to shocks and has outperformed expectations over the past quarters, it is not as dynamic as in 2022 and is more vulnerable to shocks. records.text: y? For three main reasons. First, we think the acceleration so far this quarter is partly driven by tariffs. Tariff pass through has been uneven, but it appears firms used the typical annual price reset at the beginning of the year to pass through cost pressures stemming from trade policy. Goods more exposed to continued to increase in January and are expected to continue that trend in February (see chart below). Goods less exposed to tariffs also increased recently, but we think that the strength in that group was mostly driven by noise in software and jewelry. Following the February CPI, we now estimate that tariffs have contributed around 60bp to prices so far. Our models suggest that current tariff levels are consistent with a total pass through of roughly 70bp, implying that the remaining tariff impulse for the rest of the year is only about 10bp. While there is wide uncertainty around these estimates, they suggest we may be close to normalization in core goods inflation ahead. Second, we think the recent strength is also explained by what we (and many others) refer to as “residual seasonality.” Residual seasonality reflects predictable seasonal patterns that persist in seasonally adjusted core PCE prices. records.text: on. What will the growth outlook look like? Based on current market conditions, we expect the MPC to be presented with marginal downgrades to GDP growth this year and next. Higher energy costs will squeeze real disposable incomes further, limiting consumption. Higher uncertainty will hit investment. Tighter financial conditions will impact spending also. And we expect any firming hiring plans to be delayed further, dampening activity. Based on similar elasticities used in the May 2022 MPR, we estimate current market moves to lower GDP growth by 0.25pp in 2026, 0.1pp in 2027, and an unchanged 2028 GDP growth rate. Undoubtedly, the MPC will also explore a range of scenarios to assess the outlook for demand. Similar to our own analyses, we think the forecasts could be wide- ranging. A sustained rise in energy prices, or an escalation in price momentum, would lead to even larger falls in output, adding to an already widening output gap. What will the MPC be seeing on the labour market? The weaker starting point on the quantities side of the labour market probably will already be worrying for the MPC. We expect January data to show a further increase in the jobless rate to 5.3% – a report the MPC will have had early access to. We expect the central bank to remain on hold for now before resuming rate cuts in mid/late Q2. An important caveat to this rests on avoiding the worst-case scenario in the Middle East given Türkiye’s high energy sensitivity. In this instance, the bar to resume rate hikes is likely the region’s lowest. Price control mitigants can limit the worst case: The government has already introduced a temporary fiscal instrument to offset the effect of higher fuel prices on consumer inflation. Following the same framework, which was employed during previous episodes of high oil prices and TRY depreciation, officials are lowering the Special Consumption Tax (SCT) on fuel products. The SCT has generated roughly TRY50bn in fiscal revenues over recent months. Consequently, exhausting the entire SCT buffer would cost less than 0.1 % of GDP/month. The burden on public finances would therefore be limited, especially given low rollover ratios and improved budget performance (see TURKGBs: Technicals imply a flatter yield curve, dated 27 January). Data on oil reserves and consumption varies greatly across different sources. This may reflect differences in data definitions and collection methods – i.e. the data may cover crude alone, or include products and gas; it may relate to commercial and/or strategic reserves and be self-reported or rely on satellite-derived tracking. Some data may also be adjusted for anticipated energy rationing. Looking across these measures though, we tend to find a similar distribution in reserve/consumption ratios across Asia: China, South Korea and those less reliant on energy imports (Malaysia and Indonesia) tend to hold larger reserves relative to their consumption needs, while India, Thailand, and Singapore tend to hold much less, which could make them more vulnerable during supply- driven shocks (Figure 5).
